#42359. Why Southwest Airlines Might Change Its Cabin Interior Again

Why Southwest Airlines Might Change Its Cabin Interior Again

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1433 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Southwest Airlines completed the fleet-wide reconfiguration of its cabins to add extra legroom seating earlier this year.
  • The project was massive in scope, but the work itself was light and was even completed a week ahead of schedule.
  • Recent findings suggest that today, there are now premium seating options, and passengers are paying to select specific seats online.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Southwest Airlines completed the fleet-wide reconfiguration of its cabins to add extra legroom seating earlier this year. The 737 MAX 8s and 737-800s left the shop essentially the same as when they entered, but with the seat pitch adjusted to add the extra legroom section, while the 737-700s have lost one row to make room for the extra legroom seats.

The project was massive in scope, but the work itself was light and was even completed a week ahead of schedule. The reconfigurations represent the start of a latest era at Southwest, in which the famous 'open seating' policy has been discontinued.

Recent findings suggest that today, there are now premium seating options, and passengers are paying to select specific seats online. The final Southwest flight with open seating, operating from Honolulu to LAX, departed on January 26, and when it arrived the following morning, Southwest was just like everyone else. However, could another interior modification be on the cards?

Recent findings suggest that southwest has recently changed the configurations of its entire 800+ Boeing 737 fleet. The primary change was to adjust the seat pitches of each aircraft to create a dedicated section of extra legroom seats. While the newest Boeing 737 MAX 8 deliveries feature Recaro R2 seats with special seat covers to denote that they offer added space, these seats will be largely indistinguishable on most aircraft.

In a recent development, this is because special seat covers have not been applied to the Collins Meridian or Innovator II seats found on older aircraft. The 737-800s and 737 MAX 8s are maintaining their maximum capacity of 175 seats, but 45 of these seats now feature 36 inches (91.44 cm) of legroom, per aeroLOPA.

Industry observers note that the 737-700s, previously configured with 143 seats, will now feature 137 seats, as the thickness of the older Innovator II seats meant that a row had to be sacrificed to make room for the extra legroom seats. 40 of these are extra legroom seats, boasting an exceptional seat pitch of 38 inches (96.52 cm). Currently, only new 737 MAX 8s, along with some reconfigured 737-800s, feature the Recaro R2 seats.

In a recent development, the rest of the 737 MAX 8 fleet and most of the 737-800 fleet are equipped with the Collins Meridian. Meanwhile, some 737-800s, along with all 737-700s, are equipped with the B/E Aerospace (now part of Collins) Innovator II. Some 737-700s will be retrofitted with Collins Meridian seats, and all 737-800s with the Innovator II seats will receive the Recaro R2. All planes with the R2 feature in-seat power, and all aircraft with the Collins Meridian will be retrofitted with in-seat power.

Sources indicate that southwest's CEO Bob Jordan has confirmed that his company is seriously looking into adding a first class cabin onto its planes. No official announcement has been made since Jordan commented on this idea in January, and looking into a new cabin is hardly the same as a confirmation.

Industry observers note that however, in the current state of the US market, as well as Southwest's trajectory, Jordan's comments are essentially a confirmation that a first class cabin on Southwest is a matter of when, not if. Naturally, any details as to what this could look like are pure speculation. The company is partnering with Recaro for its newest economy seats, so the Recaro R4 or R5 would be the frontrunners.

36 to 38 inches (91.44 to 96.52 cm).

33 to 34 inches (83.82 to 86.36 cm).

Southwest is retrofitting its aircraft with in-seat power as well as Wi-Fi, so you can expect these amenities, but seatback entertainment is extremely unlikely. The carrier's pitch for extra legroom seats is among the best in the industry, so some inches would likely be taken out to make room for first class seats. Southwest Airlines traditionally positioned itself as a hybrid carrier, blurring the lines between a low-cost carrier and a legacy airline.

It has been revealed that now, however, budget airlines are increasingly moving upmarket as that's where the money is. Spirit long offered a stripped-down first class product called 'Big Front Seat' before its collapse, and Frontier is now also preparing to debut a latest first class product. JetBlue, meanwhile, is working on a domestic first class product titled 'Mini Mint.'.

According to recent reports, in any industry, premium products generally sell for high margins, but of course, face a smaller market than mainstream products. In the US airline industry, however, the market for premium seating has increased dramatically. As such, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines, and Alaska Airlines have been making all of the money.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, the rest (including American, which strategically moved downmarket before COVID) have been left behind. This is tied to the increasing importance of loyalty programs, which are the primary profit centers at Delta, United, and Alaska. Customers want to earn miles and use airline-sponsored credit cards so that they can then fly in Delta One, travel to Cape Town with United, or book an award ticket with an Alaska Atmos partner.

Industry observers note that earning Southwest Rapid Rewards points for redemptions in economy within the US simply doesn't have the same appeal, and so consumers are moving to the legacies. Adding a first class product increases the appeal of Southwest's Rapid Rewards program and gives potential loyalists more incentive to build status with the carrier.

Sources indicate that first class seats are also higher-margin products than economy seats as a whole. Being cheap no longer sells, which is why the ultra-low-cost carriers are adding premium products, and Southwest's previous brand image of being a quirky airline with a uniform onboard product at largely affordable prices also doesn't cut it today.

There can be no denying that after Elliott Investment first boarded the airline in June 2024, it fundamentally changed Southwest's business model. Before Elliott, Southwest did not offer premium seating, it gave two checked bags for free, there were no airline partnerships, bookings could only be made on Southwest's website, there were no assigned seats, and no redeye flights.

Sources indicate that elliott aggressively argued that this needed to change. It is true that Southwest's finances greatly lagged behind industry leaders coming out of the COVID-19 pandemic, and the carrier had also been suffering from antiquated systems as well as outdated practices. Southwest's operational and sales changes, as such, have been a net positive.

Sources indicate that however, many of the customer-facing changes have been controversial, to say the least. Southwest is now charging for previously complimentary services like checked bags, and it now assigns seats to passengers. Under Elliott, Southwest has been chasing ancillary revenue and attempting to move up-market with its premium seating options.

In a recent development, however, before the COVID-19 pandemic, Southwest had recorded nearly half a century of straight profits. This was possible because Southwest's unique attributes, such as open seating and two free checked bags, garnered it a cult following. This customer base kept Southwest in the green during previous downturns, but Southwest, under Elliott, has decided to shun its most loyal followers in favor of following industry trends.

According to recent reports, southwest is now just like every other airline in the US, and the former loyalists now have no reason to stick with the carrier. Instead, the carrier is targeting a wider audience and offering an increasingly diverse selection of seating options to cater to a more premium clientele. It's competing mainly on price, schedule, and network.

According to recent reports, while boosting ancillary revenue has increased the carrier's short-term financials, it's not sustainable to rely on this long-term. Without Southwest's former cult following, the carrier has to commit fully to its premium shift, even once Elliott Investment has left the firm. First class is as popular with travelers as ever, and delaying Southwest's entry into this market space simply leaves money on the table.

Southwest Airlines' Interline Partners.

According to recent reports, furthermore, the presence and availability of the product will make Rapid Rewards a more desirable loyalty program, a goal that Southwest has already been working towards with its foreign airline partnerships and changes to its credit cards. It's unclear when Southwest will commit to this move or how the product will look.

In a recent development, ​​​​​​​However, the US airline industry is shifting towards one dominated by premium products and loyalty programs. Southwest, looking to emulate the profits made by the nation's most successful airlines, is adapting to emulate their business models. As such, first class could be the next logical step.

Tech Report: 11 Best Airbnbs in Stockholm for Historic Architecture, Saunas, and Beach Access

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For a break that balances the buzz of discovering a upcoming city with a good dose of fresh air, Stockholm’s mix of lush parks and eclectic architecture is an enduring choice.
  • Industry observers note that these 11 excellent rentals throughout the city and its outskirts balance top-notch amenities with the freedom that only comes with a private booking.
  • We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a break that balances the buzz of discovering a upcoming city with a good dose of fresh air, Stockholm’s mix of lush parks and eclectic architecture is an enduring choice. The city is formed of 14 islands, meaning you’re never too far from a waterfront to amble along. It's packed with historical charm (head to Gamla Stan to see one of Europe’s oldest medieval cobbled streets), as well as stylish boutiques and museums championing everything from Abba to the world’s best-preserved 17th-century warship. While the city is home to a slew of excellent hotels, from elegant converted townhouses to the former home of Astrid Lindgren (author of the beloved Pippi Longstocking book series), you’ll want to look to Airbnb for a real home-from-home vibe.

Industry observers note that these 11 excellent rentals throughout the city and its outskirts balance top-notch amenities with the freedom that only comes with a private booking. True to Nordic form, there’s a clutch of homes with their own sauna and steam rooms, and all have either sea or skyline views. Below, the best Airbnbs in Stockholm to book for a weekend of weaving through medieval streets, gallery hopping, and lots of cinnamon buns.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Historic architecture, prime location, dedicated workspace.

Sources indicate that subverting traditional Scandi minimalist sensibilities, this cool retreat in the hip heart of Södermalm channels a moody, more underground kind of charm. On the top floor, light-flooded, open-blueprint living areas are packed with rich, creamy furnishings and crisp architectural lines—multiple previous guests say that this is one of the most stylish homes they’ve ever stayed in. Downstairs, two tranquil bedrooms are carved directly into the exposed natural rock, so you can sleep beneath historic vaulted ceilings after a long day skipping from sight to sight. On that note: Södermalm is an eclectic area of town, with plenty of vintage shops and wine bars, after which you can hole up in this cocooning, cave-like retreat, as though you’re stepping into your own secret—and very stylish—bunker.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Fotografiska, Riddarholm Church, Stockholm City Museum.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Forest access, indoor fireplace, outdoor gas grill.

In a recent development, blink, and you might miss this off-grid, A-frame cabin, hidden among a thick swathe of pine trees. It’s worth searching for: Once you make your way through the foliage, you’ll find a truly wonderful Swedish escape for two. The glass-fronted structure invites in all of the elements, while inside, it’s time to switch off—there’s a crackling open hearth where you can grill all of your meals, and precious little noise other than the rustle of wind through the canopy. Fair warning: There’s a very rustic toilet and seasonal shower about a 30-second walk down the forest path, so if you’re not a DIY fan, perhaps look elsewhere. Nonetheless, for more adventurous sorts, the trade-off means absolute tranquility surrounded by happily grazing sheep and twinkly starry night skies—all within a hop and a skip of the capital.

Neighborhood: VärmdöThings to do nearby: Lillsved Beach, Buddharama Temple, Stora Sandön.

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Historic warehouse, steps from the lake, wood-burning fireplace.

Wood-beamed ceilings, clattering floors, a muted color scheme, and a signature bright exterior welcome you in from the cold—this former warehouse just oozes 19th-century charm the moment you round the corner. Better yet, it’s totally massive, sprawling across three roomy floors, with a prime spot perched right on the peaceful banks of Åkers canal. A snazzy and social kitchen space opens onto a central island and a fireplace, where all the family will want to gather. When it’s time to bed down, there are cozy curtained sleeping nooks and an additional attic dormitory, adding a playful, rustic vibe. You can rent canoes from host Cecile to paddle down the canal, or jump on an e-bike to explore the surrounding nature reserves. When you return, fire up the outdoor grill and gather around the dining table for a long dinner with more endless views.

Neighborhood: Norrö-StavaThings to do nearby: Prästfjärden lake, Näsudden nature reserve, Åkersbro walking trails.

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Sea views, sauna, hot tub.

This joyfully bobbing houseboat turns the gray blue waters of the Baltic into something akin to your own front lawn—and it does so just 15 minutes from the heady sights of central Stockholm. Panoramic floor-to-ceiling glass means you feel that you’re virtually out on the water—and, of course, you can dive straight into the lake from your bedroom deck. Dry off and hop into the private wood-fired sauna to warm up. Hop off the boat, and you can sunbathe on the jetty, cook up some local catches on the barbecue, or jump into the complimentary canoe. All in all, this is an idyllic waterside playground that active types will love.

Neighborhood: BooThings to do nearby: Kringelgården bakery, Saltsjöbadens golf course, Artipelag.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Sauna, beach access, pet-friendly.

According to recent reports, expect some truly good seascape ASMR when you stay here—you’re so close to the water you can hear the waves rolling onto the shore right from the porch. Grab the kayak from the cupboard and head down to the beach to make the most of this beautiful location. It’s a short drive from the home to Stockholm’s city center, but you’re rewarded with much serenity and glorious views instead. For those seeking a secluded family stay, this is the place.

Neighborhood: TyresöThings to do nearby: Sandholmarna nature preserve, Tyresta nature reserve, Lilla beach.

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Wood stove, sauna, beach access.

This spacious waterside cottage is not in Stockholm’s city center, but by compromising on a 30-minute commute into town, you gain something really special. The owners took the original 130-year-old structure down piece by piece, rebuilding it on their own property. It was worth the effort. Now, it lies surrounded by pine trees in a nature reserve beside a sparkling, clear lake, with the sea just a few steps further in the other direction. A large porch provides the spot for barbecue dinners and sunbathing sessions in the summer, and there are two spas within walking distance for those looking for their Scandi sweat fix—the sea-facing Skepparholmen Spa, and Japanese onsen-style Yasuragi. But you don't have to head that far, as the property has its own sauna. Stay in as long as you can muster, then cool off by jumping in the lake—something all the more satisfactory in the winter months.

Neighborhood: BooThings to do nearby: Boobadet Beach, Nyckelvikens wildlife refuge, Sushi Bar Namiyama.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Rooftop views, beach access, pet-friendly.

A previous guest says this flat has a New York City vibe, and we can see why—the interior space is small but stylish, with an industrial bent and views all over the coolest part of Stockholm from the balcony. It’s on the top floor of this apartment block, so the vistas can’t be beat. It’s been a winner for those on work trips, thanks to superfast WiFi and a dedicated workspace, and, unusually for Airbnb stays, you can bring your dog too.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Liljeholmsviken waterfront, Högalid Church, Skinnarviksberget.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathroomWhy we love it: Steam room, in-unit washer/dryer, fully equipped kitchen.

In a recent development, for an Airbnb stay that’s as close to checking into a luxury hotel as possible, look to this plush apartment right in the city center. The whole place is brand upcoming, and no expense has been spared on the fittings—there are genuine oak floorboards, Italian travertine surfaces, underfloor heating, and a slew of top-notch furniture, plus little touches such as a shower seat and a gloriously powerful rainfall shower. The best bit is the steam room; there’s no better way to decompress after a long flight or a blustery autumnal walk by the river.

Neighborhood: VasastanThings to do nearby: Vanadislunden park, Odenplan plaza, Swedish Museum of Natural History.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Proximity to metro, private patio, in-unit washer/dryer.

In a recent development, if dopamine itself could be characterized as a building, it’d be this one. The place (all 300 square feet of it) is pure joy from top to bottom—with a pink-tiled kitchen, mint-green bathroom, and cozy bedroom nook with yellow walls and blue candy-striped bedding. Cheery artworks add a final flourish. Despite its bijou size, there’s room for two more guests on the pullout bed, and there’s a patio with twinkly fairy lights to sit out on sunny afternoons with a book, a glass of wine, or both.

Neighborhood: ÄlvsjöThings to do nearby: Älvsjö Forest Nature Preserve, Herrängens Gård, Långbro park.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Beach access, sauna, kayak.

Forget your average homely fisherman’s cottage—this home here, on the cusp of the lake in the city’s swish Stocksund neighborhood, marks a newer, more modern breed of lake house. It’s chic as anything you’ll find in the city, with smooth, polished concrete floors and knotty pine walls finished with a moody, cocooning interior palette. Sweeping glass windows make the most of the beautiful views that stretch over the water and right to the city as it twinkles on the other side. Grab the kayak and spend an afternoon bobbing on the lake, then stop in for a well-deserved sweat session in the private sauna.

Neighborhood: StocksundThings to do nearby: Restaurang Hemma, Svanholmsparken park, Swedish Museum of Natural History.

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Wood-burning fireplace, Aesop toiletries, garden view.

In a recent development, this traditional Swedish apartment has had a modern facelift recently. Now it pairs gorgeous original features, including imposing 10-foot-high ceilings and whitewashed floorboards, with a sleek new kitchen and selection of cool designer furniture pieces. There's also a truly cloudlike sofa just made for cozy nights in. The surrounding streets are just as cool as the interiors; this home is smack dab in SoFo—by far Stockholm’s trendiest district—so you're just one street over from a clutch of the best of the city’s bar, restaurant, and café scene.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Fotografiska, Stockholm City Museum, Vitabergsparken park.

JSX expands semi-private jet service in Fresh York with new Dallas route

💡 Key Takeaways
  • JSX, the boutique semi-private flight operator, is launching a newly introduced daily route between New York City and Dallas, the manufacturer announced this week.
  • It has been revealed that the upcoming service will fly to Dallas Love Field (DAL) starting on Feb.
  • In a recent development, JSX did not immediately disclose which airport in New York it plans to fly from.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JSX, the boutique semi-private flight operator, is launching a newly introduced daily route between New York City and Dallas, the manufacturer announced this week.

It has been revealed that the upcoming service will fly to Dallas Love Field (DAL) starting on Feb. 17, with one daily flight in each direction.

In a recent development, JSX did not immediately disclose which airport in New York it plans to fly from. JSX typically flies to New York’s Teterboro Airport (TEB) and Westchester County Airport (HPN), although various restrictions set by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey mean that JSX cannot publicly promote TEB as a destination.

Those restrictions limit JSX to only selling those New York flights to members of its free Club JSX program, which offers rewards and has no minimum spending or flying requirements. When logged into that platform, the new route is at the moment bookable from TEB.

Club JSX: Earn rewards and fly in comfort with JSX’s fresh loyalty program.

Sources indicate that the carrier will use its Embraer E145 aircraft on the route, which can seat up to 30 passengers in a 1-1 configuration. Introductory fares start at $799 one-way.

Industry observers note that "New York City and Dallas are two of America's most influential business and cultural centers, and we believe traveling between them should be as seamless as the opportunities that connect them,” Alex Wilcox, CEO of JSX, stated in a statement. "With this new daily service, we're bringing the simplicity, comfort, and convenience of JSX to one of the country's most notable travel corridors.".

The latest flight to Dallas is JSX second New York City expansion in as many weeks; the carrier declared new flights between New York and Boston earlier this month. The Dallas route is the tech giant's fifth route from New York — aside from Boston, JSX flies from New York to Fort Lauderdale Executive Airport (FXE); Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport (OPF); Naples Airport (APF); and President Donald J. Trump International Airport (DJT), formerly known as Palm Beach International, all in Florida.

It has been revealed that JSX operates out of 30 airports across the U.S. and Mexico and functions as a public charter service, rather than a formal "airline." This lets the carrier's flights work more like private ones — although anyone can buy a ticket, the flights use posh private Fixed-Base Operators (FBOs) instead of public airport terminals. That allows passengers to venture from curb to seat in just 20 minutes.

More: JSX eyes more turboprops and newly introduced mountain routes after strong passenger response.

The flight experience itself is equally luxurious with no middle seats, lots of legroom, Starlink Wi-Fi, complimentary snacks and drinks and checked luggage that’s returned right at the side of the plane. The carrier has a fleet of 56 ERJ-family jets and 4 ATR 42-600 turboprop aircraft. Overall, the service pitches the idea of private jet convenience for a fraction of the cost.

According to recent reports, JSX passengers used to bypass security screening, like passengers on most private flights. In 2025, the carrier implemented its own in-house screening process to address security concerns.

Bipartisan process for picking GAO chief breaks down

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept.
  • Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.
  • In a recent development, sources remarked Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., speaks during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee business meeting on Sept. 23. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Republican leaders have skipped a bipartisan deliberative process for recommending the next comptroller general to head the Government Accountability Office, as lawmakers prepare to consider a nomination for the post from President Donald Trump.

In a recent development, sources remarked Trump is planning to nominate Eric Ueland, who currently serves as deputy director for management at the Office of Management and Budget. The White House submitted ethics paperwork on Ueland — required for nominations — to the GAO, according to a source.

In a recent development, senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., on Thursday posted notice of a committee hearing Nov. 19 to examine more than a dozen presidential nominees for executive and judicial offices, including “a nominee to be Comptroller General.”.

The post identifies by name all of the nominees except the candidate for comptroller general. The post has been filled by an acting comptroller general, Orice Williams Brown, since Gene L. Dodaro completed his 15-year term at the end of last year.

The move by Paul to short-circuit the convening of a legislative commission to recommend candidates infuriated top Democrats, who excoriated the chairman in a joint statement Wednesday night. A special bipartisan, bicameral legislative commission is supposed to recommend at least three candidates for comptroller general to the president, according to statute.

Homeland Security Committee GOP staff solicited recommendations for a comptroller general from some Democratic congressional offices Wednesday afternoon, imposing a deadline of 8 a.m. Thursday, according to Democratic aides.

The president nominates the head of the GAO, the investigative arm of Congress, with the advice and consent of the Senate.

Recent findings suggest that paul pushed back on the criticism Thursday, saying, “Democrats have known about this for months and months and months.” He stated the last time the special commission made recommendations for the office, when Barack Obama was president, “Democrats submitted their own list, Republicans submitted their own list. So they can complain all they want but they just need to make their list and submit it.”.

In the past, however, the special commission convened, sought applications for the position, interviewed candidates and deliberated before sending recommendations to the president.

A 1980 law states that when there is a vacancy in the comptroller general position, “there is established a commission to recommend individuals to the President for appointment to the vacant office,” and that the commission must submit at least three names.

Under the statute, the commission includes the speaker, Senate majority and minority leaders, House majority and minority leaders, chairs and ranking members of the Senate Homeland Security and House Oversight and Government Reform committees, and the Senate president pro tempore.

According to recent reports, in 1981, for example, after the law took effect, the two congressional leaders, Speaker Thomas P. “Tip” O’Neill Jr., D-Mass., and Senate Majority Leader Howard H. Baker, R-Tenn., sent a letter to President Ronald Reagan saying the special commission had met and voted to recommend eight candidates to succeed Comptroller General Elmer Staats.

“The members of the Commission have taken their statutory responsibility seriously,” they wrote.

Reagan nominated Charles A. Bowsher, who was on the list, and he was confirmed.

According to recent reports, after Bowsher’s term ended in 1996, the commission eventually formed, interviewed multiple candidates, and deliberated for several months. Republicans controlled both chambers, and Bill Clinton was president. The members of the commission could not reach agreement, and as a result, the Republicans on the committee submitted their list to Clinton, and the Democrats on the panel submitted theirs.

Clinton also had his own list. Clinton nominated David M. Walker, who was on all three lists, and he was confirmed by the Senate more than two years after Bowsher’s departure. Walker argued Thursday against short-circuiting the commission process.

Recent findings suggest that “The position is of critical importance and the related statutory Commission process should not be circumvented," Walker noted. "Doing so would undercut the credibility of the person and the effectiveness of the GAO.”.

Walker resigned in March of 2008, when George W. Bush was still president. He appointed Dodaro as acting comptroller general when he left. The commission got going several months later, creating a website with application instructions and candidate questions.

Over the next two years, the commission interviewed some 20 candidates. Democrats and Republicans on the panel were unable to reach agreement, and Democrats, who had a majority on the commission, submitted their own list to Obama in 2010. Republicans followed up with their list.

“The Commission has been working in earnest on this undertaking for more than one year and has dedicated considerable time and effort to present you with highly qualified candidates for this key position,” then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., along with other Democratic leaders, wrote to Obama when they submitted the Democrats’ list.

According to recent reports, the Democrats’ move drew a rebuke from Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who was ranking member of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee at the time.

Recent findings suggest that collins said in a statement she was “extremely disappointed” that Democrats “abruptly ended the selection process for the next Comptroller General without a bipartisan agreement” on the recommendations. “We have had several exceptionally qualified individuals apply to be the next leader of the GAO, and it should have been possible to come up with a consensus list.”.

Obama nominated and the Senate confirmed Dodaro, who was one of four recommendations from the Democrats.

In a recent development, alaska Airlines will add four new destinations across the U.S. to its map.

But the additions come at a cost: The carrier has discontinued four recently added routes from its hub at Portland International Airport (PDX) in Oregon.

As airline executives say, every route has to earn its place financially in a carrier’s network.

As for the four upcoming destinations, Alaska will serve each of those with one daily flight from its Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) base. The additions are:.

The carrier will also add a upcoming nonstop from SEA to Guadalajara International Airport (GDL) in Mexico. Alaska will offer three weekly flights on Thursdays, Fridays and Saturdays with a 737-800 from March 18, 2027 through Aug. 9, 2027.

Alaska currently serves GDL from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and San Jose Mineta International Airport (SJC) in California's Bay Area, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium reveals.

The Seattle growth comes as Alaska builds its intercontinental offerings from the Pacific Northwest city. After launching its first long-haul flights in 2025 after its merger with Hawaiian Airlines, Alaska is building out a network of at least 15 intercontinental routes from SEA by 2030.

Next year, Alaska will offer nine long-haul routes from SEA with the addition of Athens International Airport (ATH), Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG), Kansai Airport (KIX) in Osaka, Japan, and Faaʼa International Airport (PPT) in Tahiti.

Alaska plans to grow its schedule by about 4% year-over-year in 2027, with the majority in long-haul international additions.

PDX, Alaska’s wunderkind hub of recent years, is losing four recently added routes. The airline will not resume seasonal service in 2027 to:.

Alaska continues to serve all four destinations from one of its other hubs.

Industry observers note that PDX remains one of Alaska’s fastest-growing hubs as the airline shifts connections to the Oregon city. The carrier's seats at the airport are set to increase 12% in the first half of 2027 compared to this year after a 17% increase during the same period in 2026, Cirium schedules show.

Recent findings suggest that "Portland is a story of focused smart growth that improves utility, strengthens the local franchise and captures the right traffic flows," Andrew Harrison, the chief commercial officer at Alaska, mentioned in September. "[PDX] proves that Seattle and Portland are stronger together, allowing us to serve more customers, connect more traffic and improve the efficiency of our Pacific Northwest network.".

As part of its PDX growth, Alaska Airlines opened a newly introduced, $18 million lounge at the airport in June.

Why Boeing Added Upcoming Engines To 1 Of Its 2 Longest-Running Aircraft In Production

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1461 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that inside Boeing's gigantic Washington plants, two of the longest-running jets in commercial aviation history are headed toward very different destinations.
  • Sources indicate that still, the doors have not shuttered yet, and thanks to a lifeline from Congress, the classic widebody is continuing to roll off the line with the same engines.
  • Boeing's decision to abandon the 767 results from both significant changes in the global cargo industry and commercial realities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that inside Boeing's gigantic Washington plants, two of the longest-running jets in commercial aviation history are headed toward very different destinations. Workers in Renton installed huge 69-inch CFM LEAP-1B turbofans on the 737 MAX to bring the 1960s airframe up to 21st-century standards. However, thirty miles north in Everett, Boeing is winding down production of its twin-aisle 767 in 2027, despite being decades newer with its 1980s-era engineering.

Sources indicate that still, the doors have not shuttered yet, and thanks to a lifeline from Congress, the classic widebody is continuing to roll off the line with the same engines. Inside those historic walls, Boeing’s engineers constantly push the cutting edge of aerospace technology. Yet they applied that innovation unevenly between their two oldest active product lines, pouring $3 billion into modernizing the 737 while letting the veteran 767 face its looming sunset.

Boeing's decision to abandon the 767 results from both significant changes in the global cargo industry and commercial realities. The 737 MAX's extensive wing and engine redesigns were justified by thousands of airline orders, but the 767's niche cargo demand could never justify a similar overhaul, particularly since shippers are shifting their focus to the upcoming 777-8F freighter and the 777-200F passenger-to-freighter conversions are being slowed down by a severe shortage of used donor airframes.

It has been revealed that boeing scrapped aims for a brand-new single-aisle aircraft after Airbus received over 1,000 bookings for its A320neo and former exclusive customer American Airlines threatened to defect, as Leeham News wrote. Rather, the 737 airframe, whose fundamental cabin cross-section dates back to the 1954 Dash 80 prototype, was modified with CFM LEAP-1B turbofans at a cost of almost $3 billion. In order to preserve single-aisle market dominance, the 737 MAX upgrade served as a crucial stopgap. It quickly compensated for itself with hundreds of airline orders and allowed Boeing to develop a future clean-sheet replacement.

While building the next-generation 777-8F and awaiting the availability of used passenger 777 donor airframes for P2F conversions, Boeing continued to operate the twin-aisle 767-300F as a temporary freight bridge. Freighter sales were restricted to a few dozen aircraft a year since commercial airlines switched from ordering passenger 767s to the lightweight, composite 787 Dreamliner in 2014.

It has been revealed that as global e-commerce and pandemic-era cargo demand increased, the 767-300F, powered by its reliable but thirsty 1980s-era General Electric CF6-80C2 or Pratt & Whitney PW4062 engines, performed adequately as a temporary stopgap. However, the International Civil Aviation Organization's carbon emission regulations, which go into effect on January 1, 2028, cannot be met by those older engines. After that cutoff, a temporary cargo stopgap would become a permanent commercial closure because the 767 could not lawfully comply with international routes without contemporary engines.

With the 737 MAX, massive narrowbody order volume turned an aging fuselage into a multi-decade cash engine that absorbed billions in engineering upgrades. With the 767-300F, low production rates meant Boeing treated the jet purely as a low-cost bridge to hold cargo customers until the 777-8F arrived and P2F conversion lines ramped up, willingly letting regulatory deadlines retire the commercial airframe rather than sinking fresh capital into a sunsetting program.

Recent findings suggest that by enacting a rule that exempted freight jets weighing between 396,832 and 529,109 pounds from newly introduced carbon restrictions until 2033, Congress attempted to give Boeing a crutch. This effectively shielded the 412,000-pound 767-300F. However, Stephanie Pope and Kelly Ortberg, Boeing executives, declined to rely on a complete legislative rescue. Foreign authorities in Europe and Asia could prohibit the aircraft from landing because a US exemption has no power outside the US, keeping brand-new freighters behind American borders and damaging their resale value for international carriers like FedEx and UPS.

Industry observers note that instead of leaning on political life support, Boeing chose to shut down commercial 767 production in 2027 and absorb a $400 million charge. Unlike the 737 MAX, where massive passenger volume easily funded complex structural and engine upgrades, the low-volume 767 could never justify a multi-billion-dollar overhaul. Boeing recognized that stretching an outdated freighter through domestic loopholes made far less sense than focusing its engineering muscle on programs with real global demand.

Everett's widebody engineers are advancing the next-generation 777X family toward final FAA certification in early 2027, opening the door for the upcoming 777-8F freighter, while the 737 MAX line continues to produce the high-volume revenue flow required to finance ongoing enhancements. Instead of producing geographically limited 767s, Boeing allowed the commercial line to shut down on time, keeping Everett's equipment focused on military KC-46 tankers while its new widebodies get ready to take over international cargo routes.

According to recent reports, putting new engines on the 737 was no simple bolt-on modification despite the appearance to a casual observer. The modern LEAP-1B engine featured a huge 69-inch fan, forcing engineers to stretch the 737’s nose landing gear by eight inches and mount the engines further forward and higher on its low-slung 1960s wing. Applying the same MAX upgrade formula to the 767 seemed promising on paper because both aircraft have similar profiles and basic construction, though the 767 has a larger fuselage.

Sources indicate that boeing’s engineering resources and factory tooling were already locked onto far bigger, future-ready platforms than the 767. Instead of pouring capital into a temporary bridge, Boeing preserved its engineering capacity for the next-generation 777-8F and more popular 777-200F, letting the 767 finish its final bridge run before handing its crucial air freight mission over to its successors.

Bolting a modern engine onto the 767 would require gutting the airplane’s internal structures and essentially changing every aspect. Its legacy aluminum wings were engineered to carry older engines weighing roughly 9,800 pounds each. Swapping in an advanced turbofan like the GEnx-1B would add over 3,700 pounds of extra dead weight per side. Supporting that heavy overhang would force Boeing to rebuild the wing’s internal ribs, spars, and titanium mounts, triggering a multi-billion-dollar safety certification that niche cargo sales could never pay back.

Industry observers note that the technology gap inside the engines was just as wide. 21st-century jets squeeze every drop of energy from fuel by running at extreme pressures and blistering heat, using space-age ceramic parts and single-crystal metal blades that survive temperatures above 3,000 degrees. That intense efficiency lets latest engines burn far less fuel and easily pass tough global pollution rules.

In a recent development, by contrast, the 767’s 1980s-era engines run at much lower pressures with traditional metal blades that cannot handle extreme heat. Those older thermal limits mean higher fuel burn and heavier exhaust that fail modern clean-air standards. Faced with rebuilding the entire wing just to carry heavier, hotter engines, Boeing accepted that upgrading the 767 was an engineering dead end.

Before the 2028 carbon cutoff, the commercial 767's demise was cemented by a market squeeze. After FedEx Express took delivery of its 152nd and final new 767-300F in May 2026, only 15 civilian orders remained on Boeing’s books, including seven for UPS and eight for an undisclosed buyer. Once those final commercial jets leave Everett before the 2027 deadline, the civil 767 will vanish permanently from Boeing’s lineup.

In a recent development, by carrying 116,000 pounds of cargo across 3,255 nautical miles without burning as much fuel as larger widebodies, the 767-300F maintained a profitable middle ground for decades. That mid-size niche is mostly gone now. While extra-large twinjets like the Airbus A350F, Boeing 777F, and forthcoming 777-8F exceed the 767 in every parameter on long-haul international routes, upgraded single-aisle freighters increasingly dominate short domestic e-commerce flights.

It has been revealed that however, a military lifeline has ensured that the Everett assembly line itself continues to operate well into the 2030s. To fulfill significant orders for the KC-46A Pegasus aerial refueling tanker for the US Air Force and allies like Japan and Israel, Boeing will keep its 767 tooling operational because defense aircraft are exempt from commercial pollution regulations. This will close a legendary commercial chapter while solidifying its future as a military powerhouse.

In a recent development, that military transformation sets the stage for the next chapter of this 1980s airframe’s remarkable survival. Outfitted with fly-by-wire refueling booms, defensive armor, and advanced cockpit displays borrowed from the 787 Dreamliner, the KC-46A Pegasus is quietly evolving far beyond its commercial roots. While the civilian 767 fades into history, its combat-ready twin is taking on high-stakes global refueling missions that will keep Everett’s assembly line vital for decades to come.

The Best Places to Go in Central and South America 2027

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this is my fourth year leading our guide to the Best Places to Go in Central and South America, and each time I’m in awe of the final result—our list for 2027 is no exception.
  • Recent findings suggest that it may be a fool’s errand to distill all this wonder into a list of just 10 destinations.
  • These are the Best Places to Go in Central and South America in 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is my fourth year leading our guide to the Best Places to Go in Central and South America, and each time I’m in awe of the final result—our list for 2027 is no exception. We’re talking about a region where the Pacific, the Atlantic, and the Caribbean converge; where the Andes reach for the Amazon; and where strings of puffy volcanoes and postcard-worthy islands stud the map like jewels. Within it all there are thriving cities where cultures ancient and modern collide head-on, and small towns that are timeless in a way that feels increasingly rare.

Recent findings suggest that it may be a fool’s errand to distill all this wonder into a list of just 10 destinations. But the places below, as singular or more broadly representative as they may be, are the region’s answer to how we are traveling right now. For example, a pioneering set of travel specialists are ready to bring you to eco-lodges that are tucked in the untamed jungle of Guyana for wildlife sightings and citizen science experiences that will broaden your understanding of the only (official) English-speaking country in South America. If you’re looking for a sport to pick up, Preá on Brazil’s northeast coast has an open invitation on kitesurfing, the wind-driven sport this fishing village has long been known for—and the reason a set of quietly luxurious boutique hotels have been cropping up within driving distance of the rolling sand dunes of Jericoacoara National Park. If wine is what moves you, then Chile’s Central Valley should be your next stop: A slew of new culinary experiences and interesting bottles from up-and-coming winemakers make this Santiago-adjacent region the trip to take in 2027. There’s also next-gen wellness in Costa Rica, quintessential expedition cruises in Ecuador, offseason trekking in Argentina, and so much more.

Get ready to max out that PTO. These are the Best Places to Go in Central and South America in 2027. —Megan Spurrell.

This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027—find more travel inspiration here.

Go for: new jungle stays, ancestral wellness experiences, and a next-level approach to ecotourism.

In the Central Highlands of Costa Rica, Finca Madre Tierra is part of a newly introduced generation of properties redefining ecotourism.

Tucked in the Monteverde Cloud Forest, Hotel Belmar's Artista Villages offers 10 bungalows in a reforestation site.

According to recent reports, half a century ago Costa Rica helped pioneer a newly introduced model of travel in the Monteverde Cloud Forest that would come to be known as ecotourism. Today the free-spirited residents of Monteverde, three hours northwest of the capital, San José, are once again redefining responsible travel—yet now the goal extends beyond minimizing tourism’s footprint to actively restoring ecosystems, supporting local communities, and forging deeper connections between visitor and place. That ethos is embodied by Artista Villas, a collection of 10 swish bungalows in a reforestation site at Hotel Belmar. Guests at the carbon-neutral property, which opened in June, engage with the surrounding jungle using in-room art kits, meet visiting artists and filmmakers at the property’s Cervecería Belmar, forest bathe in the mountain at Artista-owned Savia nature reserve, and learn about the source of their meals at Finca Madre Tierra. Calling this new form of regenerative travel ecotourism feels too small to capture its weight.

As conventional foreign-owned resorts proliferate along the nearby Gulf of Papagayo, Monteverde and the surrounding highlands continue to chart a different course. In March 2027 the working ranch and private reserve Hacienda Montezuma, located beneath the Tenorio Volcano (and normally reserved for exclusive buyouts), will launch the first in a series of wellness retreats bookable for up to 15 people. These will feature local practitioners leading equine therapy, meditation, and forest walks—all rooted in ancestral traditions. The region is also transitioning to a deforestation-free coffee model that is reshaping how one of Costa Rica's most key crops is both grown and experienced by visitors on educational tours. —Mark Johanson.

Go for: chef-led experiences, new Cachapoal Valley bungalows, and up-and-coming wine scenes.

Recent findings suggest that in Chile's best winemaking regions, there's plenty of old and new. Case in point: Chile’s most extravagant wine hotel, VIK, expanded in 2026 with eight glass-mirrored bungalows and an art-filled wellness center, with five cabins set to open next in an oak forest on the property.

Chile’s central wine valleys have long been defined by their vines—emerald rows sprawling along riverbanks, blanketing a terrain reminiscent of the Mediterranean, yet hemmed between towering Andes and a thrashing Pacific. Recently, dynamic chefs from Santiago have begun adding their touch to the region, crafting fresh culinary tours and elevating the work of emerging bodegas and wineries. Kurt Schmidt is among them. He first rose to fame crafting nine-course tasting menus at Santiago’s 99 Restaurante, built around the traditional foodways of Chilean viticultural regions. In 2027 he’ll be teaming up with the rural tourism cooperative Ruta de los Abastos (“The Supply Route”) on menu-to-territory day tours that will begin at 99 and expand out to wine valleys like Huasco, Maule, and Aconcagua, where Schmidt has spent years building relationships with vintners, cheesemakers, foragers, and fisherfolk (later multiday itineraries are in the works). Conveniently, Santiago lies just south of the Maipo Valley, which is famed for bold Cabernet Sauvignons and also home to the striking new Centro del Vino from Concha y Toro, Latin America’s largest wine producer. The 129,000-square-foot facility features contemporary art installations, barrel-side tasting rooms, and an interactive wine museum, plus access to manicured gardens and (for an additional fee) the 19th-century mansion of founder Don Melchor.

Recent findings suggest that if you have days to spare, consider heading three hours south to the Cachapoal Valley. Here, Chile’s most extravagant wine hotel, VIK, expanded in 2026 with eight glass-mirrored bungalows and an art-filled wellness center. Five cabins are next, set to open in an oak forest on the property, where winemaker Cristián Vallejo ages natural wine in clay amphorae. Continuing south, you can explore the next generation of experimental and low-intervention vino emerging from the neighboring Maule and Itata valleys, where Millennial and Gen Z winemakers are injecting fresh energy into one of South America's oldest regions at bodegas like González Bastías and Carter Mollenhauer. Add it all up and it makes for an epic wine country road trip.

As if that weren’t enough to keep you busy, know that excellent vino isn’t the only reason to dedicate your substantial vacation to Chile this year. Once you wrap up in Santiago, consider hopping over to Rapa Nui (Easter Island) for some extreme set-jetting. This remote Chilean territory in the Southeastern Pacific is the backdrop of Academy Award winner Martin McDonagh’s new film, Wild Horse Nine, and it’s sure to become a rising star on more travelers’ itineraries this year. —Mark Johanson.

Go for: upcoming conservation-minded cruises, stargazing experiences, and an endless parade of wildlife.

In 2027 National Geographic–Lindblad Expeditions will celebrate 60 years since Lars-Eric Lindblad introduced travelers to the Galápagos on the first nonscientific civilian expedition voyage, establishing the islands as a premier destination for conservation-minded exploration.

The Galápagos Islands, an archipelago of 13 major isles and over 100 rocks and inlets off Ecuador’s coast, have long attracted travelers seeking solitude and wildlife: endemic giant tortoises and marine iguanas, native scalloped hammerhead sharks, and blue-footed boobies, for starters. Nearly 97% of the Galápagos’ land area is a single national park. Visitor access remains tightly managed, making the destination one of the rare places where travelers can experience wildlife on nature’s terms (and, as scientists are learning, occasionally encounter upcoming species, like the deep-sea Microeledone galapagensis, or blue octopus). In 2027 National Geographic–Lindblad Expeditions will celebrate 60 years since Lars-Eric Lindblad introduced travelers to the Galápagos on the first nonscientific civilian expedition voyage, establishing the islands as a premier destination for conservation-minded exploration. The brand doubled its Galápagos fleet in 2025 by adding the 16-guest catamaran Delfina and the 48-guest Gemini. In January 2027 the brand will launch Ultimate Galápagos, a 13-day itinerary aboard the 96-passenger Endeavour II that visits 11 islands including remote Genovesa, known for its red-footed booby colonies. Elsewhere, Natural Habitat Adventures’ Galápagos Tortoise Camp just transitioned to 100% solar power and introduced the Galápagos’ first fully electric panga (a small skiff for excursions)—part of trips booked aboard the brand’s Petrel luxury catamaran—reducing emissions for wildlife excursions and setting a new benchmark for sustainable travel in the destination. —Hannah Selinger.

Go for: volcano trekking, peak birdwatching, price points that range from shoestring to significant spender.

Guatemala, beloved for its artisan heritage, birdwatching, and volcano trekking up peaks like the Volcán de Fuego (pictured), will continue to draw a wide range of travelers in 2027.

It has been revealed that long a backpacking destination on the Central America 101 route known as the Gringo Trail, Guatemala is an increasingly popular destination for a generation of young travelers seeking slower, more enriching tourism that won’t break the bank. INGUAT, the Guatemala Institute of Tourism, says that arrival numbers support the TikTok thesis—and are only projected to increase. Some of the appeal is timeless: Guatemalan day-to-day life is deeply steeped in ancient heritage and culture. Sprawling artisan markets like Nim Po’t in Antigua offer easy access to hand-carved and painted wood animal masks, for example, but deeper dives are offered by Antigua-based textile studio Luna Zorro, which organizes craft retreats throughout the country. The brand’s recently opened La Valiente (February 2026) is a two-bedroom guesthouse in the heart of the city, and almost everything at the property—from the bedding to ceramics—is artisan-made by local creators. The country’s natural beauty is also an evergreen draw, but as younger generations embrace the mores—and aesthetics—of hiking (and even birdwatching), trails like the rigorous two-day Acatenango trek are list-toppers in the central highland region that is ripe with some of the 780 species recorded in Guatemala. Many choose to continue to the Tikal National Park in the northeast, where 3,000-year-old ruins of the Maya city sit amid a lush green jungle setting. At the park’s recently reopened Conservation and Research Center, visitors can observe the behind-the-scenes preservation process of ruins and artifacts, only now visible to the public. It all makes for welcome news that Guatemala is getting even easier to access: Frontier is offering daily, seasonal, nonstop service from Los Angeles to Guatemala City from December 17 until January 4, if you need a last-minute holiday getaway, and United Airlines has a permanent direct route from Houston. —Anna Zou.

Go for: untamed rainforest, immersive eco-lodges, and easier-than-ever access.

Guyana still remains 85% forested, with sites like the impressive Kaieteur Falls—among the world's strongest single-drop waterfalls—awaiting travelers.

According to recent reports, guyana, South America’s only country with English as its official language, celebrated six decades of nationhood this May. Yet from a small plane bound for Kaieteur Falls, one of the most powerful single-drop waterfalls in the world, the lush rainforest below appears several geological eras older. Perhaps it’s no wonder; an impressive 85% of this country remains forested.

Most travelers start in the coastal city of Georgetown, where the country’s Caribbean identity is tangible in the annual Mashramani carnival (every February), vibrant Stabroek Market, and Gothic St. George’s Anglican Cathedral, which is made of wood. But journeys rapidly turn toward the rainforest and savanna, with Kaieteur as their most dramatic introduction. At the falls, the Potaro River drops 741 feet from a sandstone ledge—more than four times Niagara’s height—yet just over 8,000 people see it each year, usually on a day flight from Georgetown. A fuller interior journey requires a separate, multiday circuit through Iwokrama International Centre for Rainforest Conservation and Development (IIC), a nearly million-acre reserve managed alongside 20 Indigenous communities, and into the North Rupununi, a landscape of savanna, wetlands, and river villages where Indigenous-led conservation becomes part of the itinerary. For in-the-know travelers, right now—when a host of latest expeditions and accommodations have risen to meet vanguard voyage interest—is the time to go.

On that circuit, three conservation-linked stays give travelers a direct role in the work. Atta Rainforest Lodge is the base for Iwokrama’s canopy walkway, suspended 100 feet above the forest floor and managed by the reserve in partnership with Makushi communities and local tourism operators. Further into the North Rupununi, road and river lead to Rewa Eco-Lodge, operated by Rewa Village, where anglers help measure and tag arapaima before release. Another tributary leads to Yupukari’s Caiman House, a village-run guesthouse and research station where visitors help researchers study black caiman after dark. The community also raises yellow-spotted Amazon river turtles for release. Reaching these stays still requires small planes and long road-and-river transfers, though one key link is easing: In August 2026, Jags Aviation added a 19-seat turboprop service four days a week between Georgetown’s Eugene F. Correia International Airport and Lethem.

Back in Georgetown, the arrival of international hotel brands marks a new era at the start and finish of any trip. The 152-room AC Hotel opened in December 2025, with the 172-room Four Points by Sheraton following in April 2026. A Hilton resort is due on the seafront in 2028. And there are more reasons to linger in 2027: From October 8 to October 17, the capital will also host Carifesta XVI, which will return the Caribbean Festival of Arts to its 1972 birthplace, promising a cultural counterpart to the wilderness of the interior. —Paul Jebara.

Go for: latest off-season expeditions, and a slate of fresh lodges.

For the first time in 2026, tour company Hielo & Aventura offered its popular ice hiking excursion atop the Perito Moreno Glacier—in winter.

Los Glaciares National Park, with its toothy granite spires, windswept steppe, and glaciers that crack and roar as they calve into milky-blue lakes, has long been the crown jewel of Argentine Patagonia. Yet its main gateway town, El Calafate, hasn’t seen a newly introduced luxury hotel in over two decades. That changes in December 2026 with Explora El Calafate, an all-inclusive 20-key lodge snaking across a Patagonian estancia near Lake Argentino. The hotel’s design leans into soothing earth tones—with giant windows framing distant glaciers—while menus highlight Patagonian lamb, trout, and wine. Guides take guests on 30 different adventures out to remote wildlands like the ice fields of Brazo Sur or the bird sanctuary of Laguna Nimez. Explora will simultaneously open a second property just across the Chilean border in its private Torres del Paine Conservation Reserve, further linking the two destinations by building out a binational circuit.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, southern Patagonia is shedding its reputation as a summer-only destination. Awasi Patagonia, near Torres del Paine, will now remain open through the 2027 winter season—prime time for puma safaris—while ecotourism operator Chile Nativo extols the virtue of the offseason with its Winter W Trek, tracing the iconic route past Paine Grande and the Grey Glacier in the region’s quieter season. The momentum is even greater in Los Glaciares. In 2026 park concessionaire Hielo & Aventura, responding to greater off-season demand that can help disperse the annual tourist traffic, operated its popular ice hiking excursion atop the Perito Moreno Glacier during the winter for the first time. Unlike most Patagonian mountain towns, El Calafate doesn’t shut down when crowds depart, which means there are still hot chocolates to be had after a day on the ice. —Mark Johanson.

Go for: a buyout villa in jaguar country, and groundbreaking conservation efforts.

Caiman’s newly introduced private villa, Cordilheira, has seven bungalows with buyout options for larger groups, offering a new way to stay in this wildlife-rich corner of Brazil.

For flora and fauna lovers headed to South America, the Amazon has long been the marquee trip. But further south, where the waters of the Amazon trickle down into the world’s largest tropical wetland, something different awaits. The Pantanal stretches across 42 million acres in Brazil, Bolivia, and Paraguay. In comparison to the Amazon, it’s a bit more arid, with strong cowboy culture, and the foliage is sparser, making this a great place to spot jaguars in the wild. This is in no small part thanks to notable conservation work that has taken place over decades. At the upscale Caiman Pantanal, a trailblazing safari stay in the Brazilian Pantanal, jaguar rescue group Onçafari has an on-site location, allowing guests at the all-inclusive property to explore 131,000 acres of land with the major cat experts who have meticulously tagged and tracked dozens of them. Caiman’s newly introduced private villa, Cordilheira, was unveiled in June 2026. It brings together seven bungalows (private infinity pools included) that fit up to 16 people, making it possible for families and groups to have a buyout experience as they spend days tracking jaguars—and tapirs, and giant anteaters, and capybaras—before evenings filled with Brazilian barbecue and folk music under the stars. Operators like Natural Habitat Adventures can continue the journey northbound to destinations like Porto Jofre, where cat sightings happen by boat on the river, and jaguars can be seen chasing caimans at the water’s edge. The conservation work required to protect this rare natural landscape and its fauna is ongoing, but new projects like the Jaguar Rivers Initiative, announced in fall 2025, prove the only way is forward. This new coalition, which connects the aforementioned Onçafari with Kristine Tompkins’s Fundación Rewilding Argentina, Nativa in Bolivia, and Fundación Moisés Bertoni in Paraguay, hopes to better link and restore various jaguar habitats. The goal is, of course, ecological first and foremost—but if the preservation work in Pantanal has taught us anything so far, it’s that great conservation can lead to great wildlife experiences. —Megan Spurrell.

Go for: uncrowded surf spots, a noteworthy beach hideaway, and plenty of seafood.

Opened in February 2026, resort Inkaterra Cabo Blanco overlooks the Pacific Ocean on a coastline frequented by Marilyn Monroe and Ernest Hemingway.

The seaside towns and villages of Peru's northern shore are known for their seafood dishes, such as picante de mariscos and raw-fish tiraditos.

On Peru’s northern coast, life moves slowly in the seaside towns and fishing villages that have long drawn a quiet trickle of visitors including surfers chasing mythical waves, Limeños lured by closer-to-the-equator sun and tranquility, and culinary-minded travelers who know that nowhere else does seafood quite like this part of the country. In the past few years, an increasingly stylish crop of Airbnbs have popped up—like Kahu Beach House in Los Órganos, where modern design uses endemic natural materials and where fantastic surf breaks are visible from your breakfast table. The more recent resort opening of Inkaterra Cabo Blanco in February 2026 has shone an even brighter spotlight: On the same stretch of sand where Marilyn Monroe and Ernest Hemingway vacationed in the 1950s, this contemporary beachside stay with just 13 rooms is an elegant approach to the destination’s barefoot ease, refined coastal dining, and experiences that range from a day on the water with a local fishing collective to surfing and kitesurfing lessons just steps from the private plunge pools. As for the region’s culinary offerings? You won’t have to look hard. This sun-baked stretch of coast is where carne seca dries on clotheslines and makes its way into seco de chavela (a pounded beef and plantain dish bursting with chile), and where Peruvian classics like conchas a la parmesana (scallops baked with cheese) are remixed using conchas negras, a unique shellfish found in the mangroves of Tumbes, near the border with Ecuador. Hearty dishes like picante de mariscos, a seafood stew, sit side by side with chilled raw-fish tiraditos that fly close to the sun in their spice. —Megan Spurrell.

Go for: kitesurfing for pros—and newbies—in a fishing village now home to quietly luxurious stays.

With the charm of a fishing village and powerful winds, Preá has become an ideal kitesurfing destination.

From spa treatments to horseback riding and yoga Preá's hotel scene brings a bevy of activities to travelers.

Preá has the unmistakable charm of a Brazilian fishing village—a seemingly endless shoreline, a sandy-street village center, and beachfront restaurants serving fresh-caught seafood—with one major difference: wind, and lots of it. From July through early January, this sleepy town catches some of the world’s most consistently powerful gusts, the kind kitesurfers cross oceans for. Now, with the sport growing in popularity, beginners are starting to come too, bringing with them an exciting new energy. Kitesurfing has become so popular among Brazil’s well-heeled travelers that Marco Dalpozzo, a partner at the pioneering pousada Rancho do Peixe, dubbed the sport “the new golf, the new tennis, the new skiing.” Learning takes some commitment: First-timers start on the sand before progressing into the water, with a full beginner course happening over several days. Yet new kitesurfing locations are making it easier than ever for newcomers to join the scene.

In a recent development, while the famed Jericoacoara next door is known for its lively nightlife and parties, Preá’s newly introduced crop of high-end boutique hotels and villas offers a more exclusive take on barefoot luxury. Think ocean-facing rooms, intimate private villas, and seaside bungalows paired with their own kite schools, full-service spas, and feet-in-the-sand restaurants. Whether you’re up for braving the wind or not, there is plenty else to do in terms of both adventure and restorative wellness.

Preá offers easy access to the landscapes that made neighboring Jericoacoara famous. Set off by buggy or quad to explore the region’s enormous sand dunes and freshwater lagoons that naturally occur between them, or visit the otherworldly Jericoacoara National Park. Back in Preá, book a treatment at L’Occitane spa at the Preabeach Boutique Hotel, take advantage of the yoga offerings at Hotel Kabana, or horseback ride along the shore. By sunset, everyone gathers on the beach to watch the last kiters streak across the water as what looks like a giant ball of fire slips into the ocean. Later, dinner can range from candlelit seaside dining to charming restaurants like Casinha in the rustic village center, where flip-flops are acceptable attire.

The wind is bringing in major investments too. Grupo Carnaúba is building what it envisions as the wind sports equivalent to an Alpine ski resort. Its members-only Carnaúba Wind House, opened in 2024, offers bungalow stays with a kite center, beach club, restaurant, and freshwater lagoon, while the larger Vila Carnaúba development is adding more luxury residences and beach tennis facilities. The biggest arrival yet comes in 2028, when Anantara opens its first property in the Americas: A beachfront resort complete with its own signature spa and dedicated kitesurfing school. —Carla Vianna.

Go for: cheffy restaurant openings, a revitalized downtown, and a lineup of literary festivals.

Bachour by Mata (above) is pastry chef Antonio Bachour's first Latin American pastry shop—and it joins a wave of buzzy culinary openings that have made this city an increasingly hot food destination.

According to recent reports, são Paulo is a city for those with an appetite—for business, culture, and, of course, food. Brazil’s largest and most frenetic metropolis is home to some of Brazil’s most extraordinary architectural landmarks, from Lina Bo Bardi’s museum of art (MASP) to Paulo Mendes da Rocha’s reimagined Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo. Meanwhile, the restaurant landscape has never been more exciting: São Paulo is now home to the only two restaurants in the Southern Hemisphere recently awarded three Michelin stars: Tuju and Evvai.

That momentum is reshaping the city well beyond its established dining districts: Near Avenida Paulista, the Mata São Paulo hospitality complex has gathered some of the city’s buzziest names, including Mata Città, Korean barbecue spot Lavva, and pastry chef Antonio Bachour, who opened his first Latin American pastry shop Bachour by Mata here, all in one place. More is on the way, including a newly introduced boteco, Á Brasileira, from Janaína Torres (named the World’s Best Female Chef in 2024 by World’s 50 Best). Her beloved Bar da Dona Onça, on the ground floor of Oscar Niemeyer’s sinuous Copan building, has itself gained new neighbors, including seafood-focused Brisa do Barú and Tem Umami!, an ice cream shop with a near-permanent line out the door. Together with an observation deck, the new arrivals are turning the 1,160-apartment Modernist landmark into one of downtown’s liveliest destinations.

It has been revealed that also inside the Copan is Livraria Megafauna, part of a new wave of independent bookstores bringing literary life back to São Paulo’s streets. Its Poesia no Centro poetry festival, returning in April 2027, has already become a fixture on the city’s cultural calendar; meanwhile the growing Feira do Livro, organized by literary magazine Quatro Cinco Um, is expected to draw around 100,000 people to the Praça Charles Miller in May 2027, and it will nearly double the space devoted to its mostly independent publishers.

That literary boom is part of a broader cultural surge, with major events like SP-Arte in April and the Bienal de São Paulo—Latin America’s largest visual arts event—returning to Ibirapuera Park in September. The expansion of Museu de Arte de São Paulo Assis Chateaubriand, the city’s landmark art museum, only adds to the momentum: Its newest building, opened in March 2025, increased exhibition space by more than 60% and made room for new indicates and works from the collection previously kept out of public view. —Rafael Tonon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taiwanese carrier Starlux is branching out to Australia and Newly introduced Zealand with a new, one-stop connection.

Starting March 23, 2027, the airline will fly from Taipei to Sydney to Auckland. Flights will initially operate four times weekly, then switch to daily on May 1. Starlux will operate the route using Airbus A330-900 aircraft.

Taipei-Sydney-Auckland will be the airline’s first one-stop or through route; all other flights are nonstop from Taiwan. Officials stated the one-stop approach will give travelers access to “two incredible destinations in one journey.”.

Starlux remarked it is working with Qantas to arrange connecting flights to other destinations in Australia, New Zealand, and Fiji.

According to recent reports, starlux is headquartered in Taipei and mainly flies within East and Southeast Asia, though it also offers service to North America and Europe. In the U.S., it serves Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, Phoenix, and Ontario, California.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries tells Fox News that he is going to speak to every member ahead of leadership elections to rally support to be selected as Speaker of the House.

House Democrats selected Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., as their nominee for speaker of the House in the 120th Congress following the party's sweeping midterm victories, a senior House Democratic staffer confirmed to Fox News Digital.

According to recent reports, despite growing opposition from progressives over his leadership and ties to the Democratic establishment, Jeffries survived the secret-ballot vote on Wednesday in a "landslide," according to the staffer, advancing him as the party's nominee to lead the majority in the fresh Congress. Only 11 Democrats voted against his speaker nomination.

The New York lawmaker must now win a full House vote in January to secure the position.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks during a press conference on Capitol Hill on Nov. 3, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images).

SENATE DEM CHALLENGING SEN CHUCK SCHUMER FOR LEADERSHIP POST BACKS HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR HOUSE SPEAKER.

Jeffries ran unopposed for the nomination, although recent reports indicated Democratic congressional offices had been inundated with calls from frustrated voters urging lawmakers to select an alternative candidate.

After he cleared the vote, the committee room where the incoming class of Democratic members, made up of re-elected and newly elected caucus members, erupted in cheering and clapping immediately following the vote.

"It was a blowout number," Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., told Fox News Digital after the vote.

The Democratic leader has faced criticism from progressive members of his party over his support for Israel and his ties to corporate political action committees, which critics argue reflect the priorities of the Democratic establishment rather than the party's progressive base.

Rep.-elect Don Leonard, D-Ohio, who flipped a district carried by Trump in 2024, told local media that he would be "shopping for a newly introduced leader" if Jeffries did not commit to changing his position on Israel.

Sources indicate that when asked by Fox News Digital if he voted against Jeffries on Wednesday, Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., a new member of the progressive caucus, declined to comment. After the vote count was reported, it was confirmed that Hamawy voted against Jeffries’ nomination.

In a recent development, rep. elects Darializa Avila Chevalier, D-NY., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donavan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, PA, and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., joined Hamawy in opposing Jeffries.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks with reporters as he walks to his office after a press conference at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on March 27, 2026. (Samuel Corum/Getty Images).

FOLLOW THE LEADER: DEMOCRATS FACE PARTY BATTLE AS DIVISIONS DEEPEN.

Sources indicate that rep. Jonathan Jackson, D-Ill., told Fox News Digital that the members who voted against them were "unfair" as they had never seen his abilities as a legislator, minority leader and let alone Speaker of the House.

Jackson added that these new representatives probably voted against Jeffries because they were following what their constituents wanted them to do.

Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told Fox News Digital that these new representatives are members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), not the Democratic Party, and have their own independent legislative agenda outside that of the establishment.

After the vote, the coalition who voted against Jeffries released a statement claiming that they opposed Jeffries' nomination because the minority leader does not represent the agenda they believe in, which includes abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Medicare-for-all.

Democrats are preparing to use their latest majority in January to immediately launch investigations, challenge President Donald Trump's policies through legislative oversight and hold congressional hearings. If Jeffries advances to speaker, he will lead that effort.

Despite the opposition, Jeffries has maintained support from prominent Democratic leaders, including former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who publicly backed his bid for the speakership.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., talk on the House floor on Jan. 6, 2023. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images).

According to recent reports, jeffries' nomination does not guarantee that he will become speaker when the fresh Congress convenes in January. The New York Democrat must still secure enough votes from the full House to win the position, but with the overwhelming victory on Wednesday, the path to speakership appears clearcut.

The looming vote could test whether progressive dissatisfaction with Jeffries' leadership translates into opposition on Capitol Hill or remains largely confined to grassroots activists.

The controversy also raises questions about whether incoming Democrats who campaigned against the party's establishment will ultimately support its chosen leader or demand policy concessions in exchange for their votes.

Sources indicate that during the secret ballot session on Wednesday morning, Democrats selected Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to become the party's next caucus chair.

Trump’s ‘invasion’ asylum ban to face justices

💡 Key Takeaways
