  • The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

Recent findings suggest that the Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

Industry observers note that “The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition claims.

Trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Sources indicate that immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”.

Recent findings suggest that last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

It has been revealed that the case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

Industry observers note that the case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The cause of the tower closure has not been officially confirmed, although sources suggest it was likely caused by a staffing concern.
  • It has been revealed that as first reported by CBS LA, the situation occurred on Wednesday evening.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that pilots flying into and out of Hollywood Burbank Airport (BUR) had to coordinate their own takeoffs and landings on Wednesday evening after the airport's control tower went 'ATC Zero,' meaning no controllers were on duty. ATC recordings captured pilots from Southwest Airlines and Alaska Airlines announcing their positions to each other over a shared radio frequency, a procedure normally reserved for airports without a control tower.

The cause of the tower closure has not been officially confirmed, although sources suggest it was likely caused by a staffing concern. It is the second time in just over a year that Burbank's tower has been left without controllers, following a nearly six-hour closure in October 2025 caused by absences during the federal government shutdown.

It has been revealed that as first reported by CBS LA, the situation occurred on Wednesday evening. In the ATC recordings, a Burbank controller informed aircraft that the tower was going ATC Zero and that radar services were being terminated. Pilots then switched to the Common Traffic Advisory Frequency (CTAF), where they began announcing their movements to other aircraft.

For example, a Southwest pilot can be heard reporting that their aircraft was on short final for Runway 8, while an Alaska Airlines crew announced that it was taxiing from the terminal area to the holding pad. The situation reportedly occurred at least twice on Wednesday evening, with the tower left without controllers for periods of around 30 minutes.

However, pilots were not completely without ATC support, as a controller covering the wider region continued guiding aircraft toward Burbank before advising them to switch to CTAF for the final stage of their approach. One pilot was heard telling another:.

"Hey, they have no controller right now. They're CTAF.".

CBS LA initially cited a source who said the issue was due to staffing shortages, adding that the same situation "could even happen again later tonight." The issue reportedly did occur again, with the tower going dark in 30-minute windows. There are suggestions that the interruptions were linked to mandatory rest breaks for a lone controller on duty. However, neither the FAA nor Burbank Airport has officially confirmed the reason for the repeated closures.

Recent findings suggest that the airport faced a similar situation on October 6, 2025, when its tower had no controllers for nearly six hours. On that occasion, Southern California TRACON handled operations remotely from San Diego, with average delays exceeding two hours. It occurred during a 43-day federal government shutdown, during which controllers were working without pay.

Industry observers note that burbank's airspace has been named among high-risk 'hotspots' due to the mix of helicopter and airplane movements, and its proximity to nearby Van Nuys Airport. Passengers at the airport expressed their concerns, with one telling CBS LA that it could be a safety problem if the pilots are "trying to jockey by themselves about where to land, and who goes next.".

ATC Zero is one of three designations the FAA uses, alongside ATC Alert and ATC Limited, to describe reduced or unavailable services at an ATC facility. When a tower goes ATC Zero, a neighboring facility takes over part of its workload, while pilots at the affected airport will typically announce their positions and intentions over CTAF.

Via CTAF, pilots broadcast their positions and intentions, so other crews can maintain awareness of nearby traffic. This includes announcing when they are taxiing, approaching the runway, taking off, or landing. Pilots must then rely more heavily on these radio calls and their own visual awareness to avoid conflicts.

In a recent development, although this is common at smaller airports, it is more significant when it happens at a busy Class C commercial airport like Burbank. The airport is served by several major carriers, including Southwest Airlines, Alaska Airlines, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and United Airlines, and typically handles over 100 daily flights.

    United Airlines Coming Back To A Hub It De-Hubbed Over A Decade Ago Could Be Its Biggest Domestic Bet In Years

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1369 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • United Airlines has buoyed its presence at Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) recently.
    • According to recent reports, but there is a sense of irony in the move.
    • United’s move back to Cleveland is particularly noteworthy because of its historical relationship with the airport.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    United Airlines has buoyed its presence at Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) recently. Several route additions this year have helped expand the US-based legacy carrier’s footprint in Northern Ohio to its largest in over a decade. They have also left locals with ample choice of United hubs and leisure destinations, making Cleveland an ever more crucial part of the airline’s network.

    According to recent reports, but there is a sense of irony in the move. United largely turned its back on the airport, unceremoniously winding down operations 12 years ago. This cut what was a major hub in itself from United’s network. So with the carrier now appearing to bet on the site once again in what looks to be a full-circle moment, the question is: What has changed?

    United’s move back to Cleveland is particularly noteworthy because of its historical relationship with the airport. After a merger with Continental Airlines in 2010, Cleveland became one of nine hubs for the expanded carrier, which retained United’s name. Unfortunately for the airport, this would turn out to be just one of a host of factors that would see it fall out of favor with the latest, combined entity.

    Not only was Cleveland the smallest of the nine hubs, but it was also relatively close to United’s existing gateways at Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD), as well as another former Continental base: Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR). While these fit nicely into the larger network and remain in use as hubs by United to this day, Cleveland failed to fill a significant role in the wider operation. Not least was Chicago—a huge airport in comparison, serving a far greater market—being only 315 miles (275 km) down the road.

    Behind all of this was the fallout from the 2008 financial crisis, which had hammered profitability across the industry. After United and Continental joined forces to cut costs, the unviable, loss-making Cleveland base became an easy target in the now-unified United and Continental brand’s drive towards efficiency. This came in 2014, with its de-hubbing (which was actually the second time in its history that United moved away).

    The de-hubbing did not mean United left Cleveland altogether, though. Rather, the carrier drastically scaled back on departures and rerouted connecting services elsewhere. Under prepares laid out at the time, United said average daily departures would be cut by around 60%. Some 72 peak-day flights serving 20 destinations nonstop were to be retained, it added, down from 200 and 61 beforehand, respectively.

    These fell further with time, too. By 2025, just 30 or so United flights were departing Cleveland daily. That is, until the carrier opted to expand its offerings from the base once again this year. Las Vegas’ Harry Reid International Airport (LAS), which United last flew to from Cleveland in 2024, would be served year-round with five flights a week starting in September, an announcement said in May. A winter service, running between December and April next year, would then see Miami International Airport (MIA) reappear on United’s list of destinations from the airport for the first time since 2014.

    * Myrtle Beach: 11 flights from June 4, 2027.

    ** San Juan: 26 flights from December 17, 2026, to January 11, 2027.

    *** Sarasota: 4 flights from March 13 to April 3, 2027.

    Industry observers note that owing to the additions, United’s winter schedule for this year going into next is set to cover 14 nonstop routes from Cleveland. This will be the most among any of the 10 passenger airlines that regularly operate out of the airport during the period. It will also leave United flying out of Cleveland almost 40 times a day in the meantime, taking capacity of the airport to its highest in over a decade. No doubt, this is in response to strong local demand.

    In a recent development, as Scott C. Carr, a City of Cleveland Department of Port Control assistant director, commented on the news of United’s route additions in May.

    “Strong demand for leisure travel continues to create opportunities to grow service and connect Northeast Ohio travelers to destinations they want most.”.

    This is by no means upcoming, however, with the airport having enjoyed progressively stronger footfall for some time now.

    Industry observers note that in fact, the airport’s own data shows a clear trend of improving traffic in almost every year since United’s large-scale departure in 2014, aside from an obvious slump during the pandemic. Though passenger numbers naturally dipped as United slashed services, it only took a few years for other airlines to move in, pick up the slack, and push the figures higher once more.

    Recent findings suggest that among the flurry of airlines to begin or expand operations in response were low-cost carriers Frontier Airlines and Spirit Airlines, as well as close United rivals Delta Air Lines and American Airlines, to name a few. Simply put, demand was always there, but capturing it without losing money required a different approach than the one United had committed to thus far.

    Prior to 2014, Continental — and later United following their merger — primarily used Cleveland as any other airline would a hub: to funnel passengers originating elsewhere onto flights headed elsewhere. But such an operation is complex and can come with caveats.

    According to recent reports, A major consideration is whether what are known as banked connections can be sustained. Here, airlines effectively sort their arrivals and departures into waves so that passengers have time to disembark one flight and board another. The downside is that all aircraft involved have to remain grounded for a period to give travelers time to get through the airport, which can be costly for a carrier. Alongside this, airport infrastructure and ground crews must be in place to support sudden spikes in activity as planes come and go in waves.

    Clearly, the practice was ultimately deemed unsustainable at Cleveland by United post-consolidation with Continental. Instead, a scaled-back, arguably simpler operation targeting those originating in or traveling to the area has taken its place. The bonus for United is that the fewer moving parts in a point-to-point system, compared to a hub-and-spoke model, make reacting to demand simpler — especially when the personnel and infrastructure to accommodatechanges are already in place.

    Indeed, United drastically cut back on services from Cleveland, but it did not fully scrap them. In fact, the airline remained its largest by passenger traffic, which gives some context into the weight of the de-hubbing decision on the airport. Either way, that meant United retained everything it needed to fly from the site — including a pilot base, cabin crew domicile, and maintenance facility.

    Recent findings suggest that but despite having the means in place to easily expand its schedule from Cleveland, United has found itself in a far less dominant position there today. Yes, it is still the airport’s primary carrier, but that is by no means as clear-cut as before the de-hubbing.

    Sources indicate that united accounted for a 28.84% share of Cleveland’s passengers over the year to August 2013, according to the US Bureau of Transportation Statistics. ExpressJet was the airport’s next-largest operator at the time, with a 14.60% share. Come the 12 months to August this year, United’s share was a more moderate 23.77%, while the gap to the second-largest - now Frontier with 21.47% - had narrowed drastically.

    In other words, competition has heated up, and a string of nonstop routes passengers can choose from in Cleveland are serviced by more than one carrier — hence the risk United has had to accept in moving back in. But another factor may have contributed to the decision.

    According to recent reports, spirit took the axe to its network prior to its collapse this year. This involved closing its base in Cleveland, where it had historically held a near 10% market share and from which it had even flown to the likes of Miami and Las Vegas. How much that has influenced United’s decision-making is debatable. Regardless, it has no doubt left a gap to be filled.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    We Need a Better GOP

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The old Republican establishment could be out of touch, unimaginative, and too comfortable with revolving-door practices that enriched former officeholders and staffers, among other failings.
    • Beginning in 2016, Donald Trump burned this establishment to the ground and created a fresh one that has its own myriad deficiencies, some of which echo the failings of yore; the extremely online elements of today’s establishment, for instance, have found a whole new way to be out of touch.
    • We say this not to pine for yesterday’s establishment — parties never go back, only forward — but to make the point that every party elite reaches its point of exhaustion, and that’s where the Trump establishment is now.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The old Republican establishment could be out of touch, unimaginative, and too comfortable with revolving-door practices that enriched former officeholders and staffers, among other failings.

    Beginning in 2016, Donald Trump burned this establishment to the ground and created a fresh one that has its own myriad deficiencies, some of which echo the failings of yore; the extremely online elements of today’s establishment, for instance, have found a whole new way to be out of touch.

    We say this not to pine for yesterday’s establishment — parties never go back, only forward — but to make the point that every party elite reaches its point of exhaustion, and that’s where the Trump establishment is now.

    There is a robust intramural argument on the right over how to interpret the historic loss in the midterms. We have our own views, but the most elemental need is a better GOP — one that is not beholden to the will of one man, doesn’t tolerate corruption, insists on strict adherence to the rule of law, encourages Congress to take up its allotted role in our constitutional system, rewards policy entrepreneurship on the part of officeholders, and focuses on results rather than performative provocations.

    It’s possible to imagine any number of people leading such a national party, and it could have different ideological colorations depending on that leader and underlying circumstances. All that is TBD and should be a matter of fierce debate and competition. But unless the party moves beyond today’s establishment and renews itself, it risks subsequent devastating votes of no confidence from the American public.

    Consider the issue of corruption, which was one of the biggest concerns of voters in the midterms. It is one thing for a party to suffer politically in the course of making progress on an important priority — say, stepped-up immigration enforcement. It is another to suffer from the perception — and, sadly, the reality — that politically connected people are engaged in untoward schemes for their own enrichment. The former is an inevitable political trade-off; the latter is a party’s elite feasting on its power and connections with no heed to the consequences for the larger cause.

    According to recent reports, president Trump, who has an overawing dominance over the party, is the source of many of the GOP’s current discontents. His influence is not going to drastically diminish anytime soon, and we know that many good Republicans have considered him better than the alternative, or have thrilled to his no-holds-barred assaults on the left. However one evaluates the Trump phenomenon, though, attempts to rely on the tropes that fueled his rise beginning in 2016, or ape his political style, will almost certainly fail — for the simple reasons that times change and Trump’s persona is not replicable.

    The GOP could do much worse than look to the states, where Republican governors and legislators have cut taxes, restrained spending, pared back regulations, protected unborn children, and pursued reforms of schooling and housing. One reason that Florida constituted high ground beyond the reach of the blue wave is that it has been so well governed for so long, and it has had a series of reformist Republican governors focused on results.

    At the national level, the GOP obviously needs a cost-of-living agenda that addresses high costs in health care, medicine, and education, and there’s much work that’s been done on these issues at the state level and among conservative policy thinkers. But arriving at a coherent agenda will require a seriousness of purpose and substantive focus that have been lacking for years now. That doesn’t mean the party should be dull and conventional — much can be learned from Trump’s zest for combat and vivid political branding — but it needs to recover a sense of institutional self-respect.

    The new establishment, via President Trump, has worked its way back around to what were widely considered weaknesses of the old one. Republicans were once determined to make another push for amnesty after every election loss, and now, the president has floated that idea in response to the Democratic midterm victory; Republicans were once too soft on China, and Trump has been notably conciliatory in his second term; the GOP once talked a good game on deficit spending but didn’t do nearly enough to curtail it, while we are now adding to the debt hand over fist during a time of economic expansion and relative peace; the Tom DeLay–led Republican House was much too cozy with lobbyists, but prior GOP ethical lapses have been eclipsed over the past two years.

    The old establishment had reached its expiration date and, regardless, isn’t coming back, while the current establishment is harmful to the party’s image and interests and an obstacle to change.

    As Lincoln noted, it is a time to think anew and act anew. The GOP desperately needs something fresh and different, with ideas and policies designed to meet the challenges of the day.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

    Industry News: Why The Airbus A350 Can Fly Late-Night Slots At London Heathrow That Ground Competing Widebodies

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that josh is an avgeek and pilot based in the United Kingdom.
    • London Heathrow (LHR) is one of the busiest international airports in the world, yet it is also one of the most tightly regulated when it comes to aircraft noise.
    • It has been revealed that this means that airlines must maximize every available slot while complying with some of Europe’s strictest environmental rules.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that josh is an avgeek and pilot based in the United Kingdom. He started at Simple Flying as a Commercial Aviation Journalist before taking a less writing-focused role as Content & Growth Lead for Simple Flying's Flight Tracker.

    London Heathrow (LHR) is one of the busiest international airports in the world, yet it is also one of the most tightly regulated when it comes to aircraft noise. Despite handling 83.9 million passengers and 474,029 aircraft movements in 2024, Heathrow remains legally capped at 480,000 annual air transport movements.

    It has been revealed that this means that airlines must maximize every available slot while complying with some of Europe’s strictest environmental rules. Those restrictions become even more significant overnight. Between late evening and early morning, airlines are not simply competing for scarce runway capacity; they are also competing against a finite noise budget.

    This is where the Airbus A350 has emerged as one of the industry’s standout performers. Combining an advanced composite airframe with the Rolls-Royce Trent XWB, Airbus states the aircraft is up to nine decibels quieter than competing widebodies, giving airlines a valuable advantage when operating into airports where every decibel matters.

    Unlike many major airports, Heathrow regulates overnight operations using a Quota Count (QC) system rather than relying solely on movement limits. Every aircraft is assigned a QC value based on its certificated noise performance for both take-off and landing. The quieter the aircraft, the lower its QC rating and the 'less' of the airport’s overnight noise allowance it consumes.

    The airport’s scheduled night quota period runs between 11:30 PM and 06:00 AM, when aircraft movements are tightly controlled to minimize disturbance for the hundreds of thousands of residents living beneath Heathrow’s arrival and departure corridors. Aircraft are assigned QC values ranging from QC/0 and QC/0.125 for the quietest types through to QC/16 for the loudest.

    Recent findings suggest that under current UK regulations, aircraft rated QC/4 cannot normally operate during the night quota period, while QC/8 and QC/16 aircraft are prohibited throughout the entire night period. For airlines, that makes aircraft selection a commercial decision as much as an operational one. A quieter aircraft allows operators to preserve more of their overnight quota while maintaining valuable long-haul schedules.

    Recent findings suggest that heathrow also incentivizes the use of quieter fleets through its landing charge structure, with newer Chapter 14-compliant aircraft paying lower noise-related charges than older, noisier designs. Today, more than 80% of Heathrow’s aircraft movements are performed by aircraft meeting ICAO Chapter 14 noise standards, demonstrating how rapidly airlines have modernized their fleets.

    According to recent reports, every A350 is powered exclusively by Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines, making it the only modern widebody family designed around a single engine type. The larger A350-1000 uses the Trent XWB-97, producing almost 97,000 pounds of thrust, making it the most powerful commercial engine RR has ever certificated.

    Despite that enormous output, it is also among the quietest engines in its class thanks to extensive acoustic optimization throughout its design. Aircraft noise is generated by far more than simply engine exhaust. Fan blade interaction, turbulent exhaust mixing, airflow around the nacelle, and aerodynamic friction across the aircraft all contribute to the overall noise signature heard on the ground.

    Sources indicate that rolls-Royce addressed these sources using a high-bypass turbofan architecture, advanced acoustic liners inside the nacelle and an aerodynamically optimized fan designed to reduce both fuel burn and perceived community noise. The results are reflected in the aircraft’s certification figures.

    Industry observers note that the A350-1000 records a certified take-off noise level of approximately 88.8 EPNdB, placing it comfortably within the quieter categories used by airports such as Heathrow. Airbus also states that the A350 is up to nine decibels quieter than competing aircraft when measured at the front of the cabin. Because sound levels multiply rather than add up, a nine-decibel drop sounds small on paper but actually eliminates nearly 90% of the physical noise.

    The A350 is frequently described as a composite aircraft, but the scale of its advanced construction is remarkable. More than 70% of the aircraft by weight consists of advanced materials, including 53% carbon-fiber-reinforced plastic, alongside aluminum-lithium alloys, titanium and advanced steel.

    Beyond reducing weight, these materials enable smoother aerodynamic surfaces, greater corrosion resistance and improved structural efficiency. The aircraft’s wing is equally significant. Spanning 212 ft 5 in (64.75 m), the highly flexible composite wing was designed specifically for aerodynamic efficiency.

    In a recent development, during flight, the wing naturally flexes upward under load, reducing drag and improving lift characteristics. Combined with carefully designed flap track fairings, engine nacelles and wing-body integration, these refinements also help minimize aerodynamic noise generated during both departure and approach.

    Passengers benefit from the composite structure as much as communities beneath the flight path. Because carbon-fiber fuselages tolerate higher pressure differentials than conventional aluminum designs, the A350 maintains a cabin altitude of around 5,500 feet while cruising between 35,000 and 40,000 feet.

    Sources indicate that this is lower compared with the standard of approximately 8,000 feet aboard many older widebody aircraft. Airbus also designed the aircraft to maintain higher cabin humidity, improving passenger comfort on ultra-long-haul flights while demonstrating that the same engineering choices contributing to lower external noise also enhance the onboard experience.

    Industry observers note that while the Rolls-Royce Trent XWB is central to the A350’s acoustic performance, Airbus designed the aircraft as an integrated package rather than simply attaching quieter engines to an existing airframe. From the earliest stages of development, engineers focused on reducing the aircraft’s overall community noise by refining everything from the wing profile and flap mechanisms to the engine nacelles and landing gear fairings.

    Sources indicate that the result is an aircraft that is not only quieter during take-off, but also during approach when aerodynamic noise becomes increasingly significant. Airbus indicates the A350 has a noise footprint up to 50% smaller than that of previous-generation aircraft of a similar size. That’s particularly important around airports such as Heathrow, where hundreds of thousands of people live beneath arrival and departure routes.

    According to recent reports, even modest reductions in perceived noise can have a significant impact when multiplied across hundreds of daily aircraft movements, helping airports balance growing passenger demand with increasingly strict environmental expectations. The A350’s design has also helped airlines perform well under Heathrow’s Fly Quieter and Greener program.

    Industry observers note that this ranks airlines using metrics including aircraft noise performance, trackkeeping, continuous descent approaches, and NOx emissions. Although the rankings assess airline operations rather than individual aircraft, carriers operating modern fleets that include the A350 are generally better positioned to score highly than those relying on older, noisier aircraft.

    For airlines, quieter aircraft are about far more than passenger comfort; they create valuable scheduling flexibility. Heathrow’s overnight movement limits and Quota Count system mean every late-night departure and early-morning arrival must be carefully planned. Aircraft with lower QC ratings allow airlines to operate within those restrictions while preserving as much of their available noise quota as possible for other services.

    Industry observers note that british Airways has embraced that advantage by building one of Europe’s largest A350-1000 fleets. The carrier now operates 18 A350-1000s, deploying them on routes including Upcoming York, Washington DC, Dubai, Bengaluru, Lagos and several other long-haul destinations. Many of these services depart Heathrow late in the evening or arrive early in the morning.

    It has been revealed that this makes the aircraft’s low noise footprint an operational asset as well as a passenger benefit. Virgin Atlantic reached a similar conclusion when replacing its aging Airbus A340-600 fleet with the A350-1000. Alongside reducing fuel burn and carbon emissions by around 30%, the newer aircraft also delivered substantially lower community noise.

    In a recent development, airlines including Cathay Pacific, Singapore Airlines, Japan Airlines, and Qatar Airways have likewise made the A350 a cornerstone of their Heathrow operations, combining long-range capability with one of the quietest noise profiles of any widebody in commercial service. Finnair also deploys the A350 on select Helsinki-Heathrow rotations.

    Sources indicate that passengers may never notice Heathrow’s Quota Count system, but they often notice the aircraft itself. The A350’s cabin is widely regarded as one of the quietest in commercial aviation, thanks to reduced structural vibration, extensive acoustic insulation and the naturally quieter characteristics of the Trent XWB engines.

    In a recent development, lower cabin noise makes conversations easier, improves the in-flight entertainment experience and contributes to a less fatiguing journey, particularly on flights lasting ten hours or more. The aircraft’s composite fuselage also enables a cabin altitude of approximately 5,500 feet, compared with the roughly 8,000-foot cabin altitude typical of many older aluminum airliners.

    Combined with humidity levels of around 20%, roughly double those found on many previous-generation widebodies, this results in an environment that many passengers find noticeably more comfortable, particularly on ultra-long-haul routes. These improvements have become key selling points for airlines marketing premium cabins, but they also benefit economy passengers by reducing dehydration and fatigue.

    Recent findings suggest that ultimately, the A350 demonstrates how advances in aircraft design can solve multiple challenges simultaneously. Airbus estimates the aircraft burns around 25% less fuel and produces 25% lower CO2 emissions than previous-generation aircraft of a similar size, while its quieter engines, advanced aerodynamics and composite structure also reduce community noise.

    Recent findings suggest that at airports such as Heathrow, where runway capacity, environmental regulation and neighborhood concerns are constantly competing priorities, that combination gives airlines a genuine operational advantage. The A350 is not simply a more efficient long-haul aircraft; it is one of the few widebodies purpose-built for an era in which noise is every bit as important as performance.

    • In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call).

    Recent findings suggest that former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family declared.

    In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

    As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

    “Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”.

    When McDermott announced his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”.

    It has been revealed that born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

    Recent findings suggest that he attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

    He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against new sanctions on Iran.

    Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a newly introduced life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

    Industry observers note that “I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”.

    As he mentioned, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

    Sources indicate that then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

    “The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he stated in a statement at the time.

    McDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

    “Jim McDermott was as big as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”.

    Is air travel ready for Thanksgiving? The meltdown is over, but worries persist

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (764 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It appears air travel is back on track after one of the most chaotic weekends we’ve seen at airports in years.
    • Flight schedules returned to normal this week after a rare nationwide ground stop created a nightmare weekend for flying.
    • It’s not so much a safety question — industry experts steadfastly agree that air travel is still remarkably safe.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It appears air travel is back on track after one of the most chaotic weekends we’ve seen at airports in years.

    Flight schedules returned to normal this week after a rare nationwide ground stop created a nightmare weekend for flying. More than 18,000 flights were canceled between Friday and Sunday, affecting millions of travelers. It appears there will be no spillover from that meltdown into the massive Thanksgiving travel week that’s on the horizon, though.

    The bigger concern is long-term.

    It’s not so much a safety question — industry experts steadfastly agree that air travel is still remarkably safe.

    But there are plenty of worries about the possibility of another major air travel headache like we saw this weekend.

    And that’s a stressful and costly reality whether you’re a passenger, a crew member, an airline executive or a front-line aviation worker.

    In recent years, travelers have gotten one reminder after another about how strained our aviation infrastructure is.

    For years, the Federal Aviation Administration has been plagued by both severely outdated technology and short staffing in air traffic control.

    Those concerns have grown even louder in the wake of several recent incidents.

    After 9/11, the U.S. went more than 20 years without a nationwide ground stop like the one we saw on Friday.

    Sources indicate that we’ve now seen two happen since 2023. Both instances involved outages to critical FAA systems.

    Meanwhile, the vital air traffic control workforce that directs the flow of planes in our airspace has been chronically understaffed. Controllers routinely work six-day weeks and mandatory overtime.

    Together, these problems have fueled several of the most high-profile air travel disruptions in recent memory.

    Last fall, ATC staffing was a major factor in the mass flight cancellations and delays we saw at the height of the government shutdown.

    In 2025, equipment outages plus undermanned air traffic control centers contributed to the weeks of chaos travelers endured at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR).

    In the wake of the latest technology failure on Friday, FAA administrator Bryan Bedford was asked bluntly whether he could say for certain that there wouldn’t be a repeat of this past weekend’s chaos.

    “I can say with certainty that the system is really, really old,” he told CBS News Tuesday.

    In a recent development, “Let’s not kid ourselves,” Bedford added. “This system has been fragile, and it does go down.”.

    There has been momentum to fix both problems, which have festered for decades under the leadership of both political parties.

    In recent years, the FAA has upped its air traffic control hiring efforts, in a push to reduce long-standing vacancies.

    Meanwhile, Congress last year earmarked $12.5 billion for infrastructure upgrades.

    The Department of Transportation has started that work, but says it needs a lot more money to make truly sweeping upgrades.

    The travel sector has broadly supported that request: “They need to get to 100% staffing and to have the funds to modernize the technology,” United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby wrote in a social media post Sunday.

    But securing that funding will hinge on political dealmaking in Washington, D.C., which in January will be led by a divided government.

    And however that fight ends, these problems won’t be solved overnight.

    It takes years to fully train air traffic controllers.

    And to add to the complexity, overhauling aviation infrastructure while tens of thousands of flights operate each day is painstaking work with significant consequences — even if the money is there in the first place.

    Look no further than last week’s FAA outage, where crews replacing a router apparently triggered a chain-reaction outage that upended air travel in the U.S. for days — a disruption American Airlines now counts among the most significant in its 100-year history.

    Recent findings suggest that “The transition itself needs to be carefully analyzed and tested,” said Capt. Shem Malmquist, a longtime Boeing 777 captain and visiting professor at the Florida Institute of Technology’s College of Aeronautics. “Otherwise, an upgrade intended to solve one problem can introduce another.".

    Despite all the concerning headlines, industry experts largely agree:.

    “Both things can be true,” Malmquist stated, pointing to the many safety layers that allow planes to safely operate even when problems arise.

    Keep in mind: Every plane that was in the sky during last week’s FAA disruption landed safely.

    And the move to halt thousands of flights? That was ultimately meant to protect travelers, leaders have emphasized.

    Recent findings suggest that "Passengers experience delays and cancellations, but those restrictions help keep the system safe," Malmquist noted. “That doesn’t mean the underlying vulnerabilities are acceptable.”.

    Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (776 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21.
    • Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they stated old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they stated old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

    The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

    He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

    During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the concerns were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”.

    Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from fresh software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin mentioned “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”.

    Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

    Recent findings suggest that “This is an emergency,” he stated. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”.

    The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

    Mullin mentioned the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

    “We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin noted. "Nickel and diming it together does not work.".

    Industry observers note that thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications.".

    Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment.".

    Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

    Sources indicate that the 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

    The committee’s majority stated Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a new one was built.

    Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., noted in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications challenges.

    “Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell said.

    Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

    In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and noted their committee would “thoroughly review the problems that led to this nationwide ground stop.”.

    Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

    According to recent reports, at problem in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have remarked they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

    Standing Athwart Pumpkin Tyranny

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A pumpkin spice latte is on the menu at every coffee shop.
    • Through October and November, pumpkin is in everything everywhere all the time.
    • Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

    A pumpkin spice latte is on the menu at every coffee shop. Sometimes, the drink is served in a pumpkin-shaped mug. To lure in customers for brunch, quaint cafes serving pumpkin pancakes put a chalkboard sign on the sidewalk saying, “COME IN FOR GOURD VIBRATIONS!” Each bakery has pumpkin scones, pumpkin pie, pumpkin banana bread, and pumpkin coffee cake. An attempt to order an old fashioned will be met with an invitation from the demoralized bartender, “Do you want to try our pumpkin spice old fashioned?” The pen at the bank is topped with a rubber pumpkin; this way, customers know that all the money is kept safe. Little plastic pumpkins are in the windows displays at clothing shops, or beside the cashiers (who work in front of pumpkin-flavored nicotine patches). Squashes are piled high in cardboard bins by the entrance of every grocery store. I reach for what I think is my favorite chai tea blend on the shelves — but alas! It is now pumpkin chai with an orange label.

    Through October and November, pumpkin is in everything everywhere all the time. Anything edible is infused, swirled, drizzled, and dusted with pumpkin. You cannot escape the flavor: pumpkin cereal, pumpkin protein powder, pumpkin bagels with pumpkin cream cheese. The Asian aisle has frozen Kung Pao-mpkin Dumplings. Dog treats are flavored like a pumpkin spice latte because everyone must participate, no exceptions. Longstanding favorites are replaced, so French fries are now pumpkin fries. That peculiar squash always sneaks its way into a dish, and so the stuffed raviolis have a little bit of pumpkin. Despite its omnipresence, the pumpkin surprises you: The waiter arrives at the table with a salad that is topped — just for this week — with toasted pumpkin seeds. (Of course, the utensils are wrapped in a flimsy brown napkin dotted with little orange pumpkins.) Even things we thought were reliably mint, like gum and the dentist’s fluoride, are pumpkin spice.

    Abigail Anthony is a staff writer at National Review.

    On “ Standing Athwart Pumpkin Tyranny”.

    #42328. Boeing 777X Pilots Have To Manually Extend The Wingtips Before Takeoff But Not Fold Up After Landing

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1454 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Boeing 777X Pilots Have To Manually Extend The Wingtips Before Takeoff But Not Fold Up After Landing

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1454 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the Boeing 777X's most famous new features is its folding wingtips.
    • In a recent development, the 777X is a massive upgrade of the legacy 777 airframe, featuring a fuselage stretch, a redesigned interior, newly introduced engines, and a new carbon composite wing.
    • Sources indicate that the last 11 feet (3.5 meters) of the wings on the 777X can fold upwards, decreasing the 777X's wingspan from 235 feet five inches (71.76 meters) to 212 feet nine inches (64.84 meters).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the Boeing 777X's most famous new features is its folding wingtips. They're roughly 11 feet (3.5 meters) wide each and are designed to be folded up whilst on the ground, allowing the aircraft to use the same airport facilities as older 777 models. They extend before takeoff and remain fully extended until after landing. Interestingly, it's the pilots' responsibility to extend the wingtips before takeoff, but the wingtips retract automatically after landing as the aircraft decelerates on the runway.

    In a recent development, the 777X is a massive upgrade of the legacy 777 airframe, featuring a fuselage stretch, a redesigned interior, newly introduced engines, and a new carbon composite wing. It's significantly larger than the wing on the older 777 models, meaning that it produces more lift than before. This cuts down on fuel burn and allows the aircraft to have much improved performance on long-haul services. It's one of the most crucial changes for the 777X, and the wingtips help ensure operational flexibility for the aircraft's customers.

    Sources indicate that the last 11 feet (3.5 meters) of the wings on the 777X can fold upwards, decreasing the 777X's wingspan from 235 feet five inches (71.76 meters) to 212 feet nine inches (64.84 meters). The wingtips themselves are carbon-composite and use a hydraulically driven hinge system to move between positions. The transition takes roughly 20 seconds, and once in place, electric locking pins hold the wingtips in place, preventing them from moving into the other position on their own.

    Sources indicate that the pilots control the mechanism via a simple knob on the overhead panel, while the position of the wingtips is displayed on the aircraft's EICAS screens. The pilots' pre-departure checklist actions now include switching the wingtips into their unfolded position, with the EICAS icon also displaying whether the wingtips are moving. If the crew members attempt to take off with the wingtips folded, the aircraft's master warning horn will sound, alerting them to the error.

    Curiously, while the pilots manually move the wingtips before takeoff, they do not do so after landing. Rather, after decelerating below 50 knots, the aircraft automatically folds the wingtips while the overhead switch pops into place. While it's the crew's responsibility to verify afterwards that the wingtips are folded, it's not an action they're meant to regularly perform after landing. In normal circumstances, manually retracting the wingtips after landing is not an action that crews will be expected to perform.

    Sources indicate that the main appeal of the folding wingtips is to allow the 777X to use the same gates and taxiways as prior 777 models. The plane's full wingspan pushes it into ICAO Code F standards, whereas older 777s were Code E aircraft. With the wingtips folded, the 777X has the same wingspan as older 777s on the ground, which means that the wingtips are only meant to be extended shortly before takeoff. Therefore, it's part of the pre-departure checklist that pilots run right before lining up on the runway.

    Because of how much extra span the wingtips add when fully extended, they can pose a collision hazard to other aircraft taxiing around the airport and near the runway. Therefore, the pilots are responsible for ensuring that they have appropriate clearance from other aircraft before they extend these massive wingtips. The crew are the ones watching the aircraft's surroundings and can judge when they have enough space to extend the tips without striking another aircraft.

    It has been revealed that upon landing, the wingtips are no longer necessary, and the crew would ideally fold them as soon as possible. However, the flight deck during the rollout can be a chaotic environment, as crews simultaneously need to safely decelerate the aircraft, maneuver it off the runway, and reconfigure the plane while performing checklist items. As such, the wingtips fold automatically after landing, as this reduces pilot workload. During this phase, it's not necessary for the pilots to judge when it's appropriate to retract the wingtips.

    The folding wingtips are a significant innovation. It's the first time that such technology has been applied to a commercial airliner, and it represents a major achievement to design such a system that can function safely and reliably. However, designing folding wingtips is also expensive, while the system itself adds weight, costs, and complexity. It's necessary to allow 777X operators to use the same ground facilities as other widebody types because the 777X's wingspan is otherwise much greater than the 777, 787, or A350.

    According to recent reports, the wing is all-newly introduced for the 777X, with Boeing having spent an estimated $2 billion on just this part of the program. While the outgoing 777-300ER was a hugely successful aircraft, its wing was relatively undersized for the weights that the aircraft routinely flew at on its typical long-haul missions. To compete against the A350-1000, which delivered significantly better performance and economics at roughly the same size as the 777-300ER, the 777X would need a new wing.

    Sources indicate that the wing itself is the widest that Boeing has ever built, as its span is even greater than that of the 747-8 (although the 747-8's wing is larger by area). It was necessary to give the 777X more lift during the initial cruise when fully loaded, allowing it to fly higher and burn less fuel. The aircraft also requires less thrust during takeoffs, allowing the 777X's General Electric GE9Xs to use less thrust. This decreases fuel burn and improves the engine's long-term durability. If the wing were any smaller, then the aircraft would be compromised.

    The biggest changes to the 777X are the new wing and the fuselage stretch. The wing is necessary to improve the aircraft's cruise performance on long-haul flights, which is how it will mainly be used. Meanwhile, the 777X still retains the original's heavy metal fuselage, which weighs significantly more than the carbon-composite fuselage on the A350. By stretching the fuselage, the 777X can seat significantly more passengers than the outgoing model, while the weight gain is relatively minor.

    Underneath the wings on the 777X are two General Electric GE9X turbofans. These are the largest jet engines ever built, and they also hold the record for the most amount of thrust ever produced from a jet engine. They feature a heavier use of advanced materials than any other engine before, making use of materials like ceramic matrix composites (CMCs) to deliver industry-leading thermal efficiency. This significantly cuts down on fuel burn, and the engine is a major leap forward even compared to a powerplant like the 787's GEnx.

    Boeing 787 Dreamliner (GEnx-1B).

    Boeing 787 Dreamliner (Trent 1000).

    The aircraft features a latest cabin and updated flight deck to more closely resemble the cockpit on the 787. Rather notably, Boeing has physically designed new windows that are larger and higher than those on prior models, while also incorporating a dimming function. The aircraft is also meant to have a lower cabin pressure comparable to that of the 787, which is a remarkable target considering that the 777 still has a metal fuselage. While it's a derivative of an existing type, the 777X is an extremely thorough overhaul.

    There are three variants of the 777X: the 777-8, the 777-9, and the 777-8F. However, the 777-8 has attracted very few orders, and development is on pause as a result. The 777-8F is being developed and has been reasonably popular for its market, with just over 100 orders in total. This is almost exactly the same amount as the competing A350F. Meanwhile, the 777-9's closest competitor is the A350-1000, and against the Airbus, the 777-9 has actually fared very well.

    In a recent development, the A350-1000 has received 373 orders, whereas Boeing has received just under 550 orders for the 777-9. Admittedly, 325 of these have come from just two customers (Emirates and Qatar Airways), but it's still a solid showing. The 777-9 is well-suited for airlines needing a large amount of floor space, as well as those that need to move heavy payloads across 15 to 16-hour routes. As it stands, however, the A350-1000 can fly farther and can carry more payload near the edge of the 777-9's payload-range envelope.

    Sources indicate that what has kept sales of both types slow is that many 777-300ERs worldwide are young. This is the aircraft that the A350-1000 and 777-9 are meant to replace, but there hasn't been much of a need for most examples to be retired yet. However, the 777-9 is better suited for carriers that want to upsize, as well as A380 and 747 operators. The A350-1000, meanwhile, is still highly effective as a 777-300ER replacement, although it has less floor space and seats fewer passengers.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, on December 8, Qatar Airways will finally lift off for Canberra.
    • Sources indicate that qatar Airways has little interest in flying to Canberra for its own sake.
    • In early July, the Gulf giant confirmed its return to the Australian capital, and the relaunch date is now fast approaching.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, on December 8, Qatar Airways will finally lift off for Canberra. The oneworld member last flew to the capital of Australia in March 2020, when the war in Iran forced it to stop. Multiple carriers continue to suspend routes to the Gulf because of the war.

    Sources indicate that qatar Airways has little interest in flying to Canberra for its own sake. It does so because of a regulatory loophole, which means it can increase the number of flights to major Australian cities in return for doing so. Singapore Airlines flew to Canberra until 2020, with Qatar Airways being the sole long-haul operator.

    In early July, the Gulf giant confirmed its return to the Australian capital, and the relaunch date is now fast approaching. Qatar Airways will fly daily using the 354-seat Boeing 777-300ER. This is one of various configurations of the variant, and first class and premium economy are not available. The two-class equipment has 42 QSuites and 312 seats in economy.

    According to recent reports, qatar Airways' schedule is as follows, which is, of course, timed for connectivity in Doha. When the resumption was disclosed, only four weekly services were planned. Obviously, no traffic rights exist between Melbourne and Canberra. Eighth freedom traffic rights, or cabotage, are rarely granted. Analytic Flying reveals that the Melbourne-Canberra-Melbourne legs have been nearly empty.

    Schedule For December; Local Times.

    When the service returns, Qatar Airways will have two flights to Melbourne, with that frequency last available in March. Virgin Australia operates daily between Melbourne and Doha using Qatar Airways' 777-300ERs for the Middle Eastern operator (it also flies from Brisbane, Perth, and Sydney). Both of Qatar Airways' daily flights to Melbourne will continue elsewhere. One will go to Canberra, while the other will fly to Auckland, replacing the one-stop service via Adelaide.

    Qatar Airways can fly to Australia's four main cities (Brisbane, Melbourne, Perth, and Sydney) up to 28 times weekly. It has used up this allowance, which is why Virgin (which leases some of the Gulf airline's 777-300ERs) flies to Doha on its behalf using the Australian half of the traffic rights.

    Sources indicate that qatar Airways itself could grow its presence in Australia by reducing the number of flights to specific airports and redeploying the allowance. This would not be appealing, as it would reduce its market share and competitiveness. It could also upgauge aircraft. The Airbus A380 was last used to Sydney in March 2026, while Perth saw it until April 2025 and Melbourne until 2020. However, market share advantages mainly come from having higher frequencies.

    The carrier decided on a different approach. By continuing to a regional city, which includes the country's capital, it is able to increase the number of flights to the major cities. No frequency limit exists with this option. This is why Qatar Airways originally flew to Canberra via Sydney, which then switched to Melbourne. It could increase flights to Sydney/Melbourne without reducing them elsewhere. It is also why the carrier previously served Adelaide through Melbourne.

    Industry observers note that when Qatar Airways and partner Virgin are combined, the pair blueprint up to ten daily nonstop departures to Australia between December 2026 and next October. To avoid double counting, the add-on to Canberra is excluded from the calculation, as there is only one takeoff from Doha.

    Qatar Airways' Flights (January 2027).

    Virgin's Flights (January 2027).

    Daily 777-300ER (via Melbourne).

    Two daily 777-300ER (one continues to Auckland, the other to Canberra).

    Industry observers note that notice that Virgin will now fly from Sydney two times a day, supplementing Qatar Airways' daily offering. This materialized as the Australian operator reduced its flights from Brisbane and Perth. By doing this, Virgin keeps within limit of 28 weekly departures on its side of the air service agreement.

    • It’s become something of a truism that the pro-life movement lacked a initiative for how to pursue its goals after Roe v.

    • John Gerardi is the executive director of Right to Life of Central California in Fresno.

    It’s become something of a truism that the pro-life movement lacked a initiative for how to pursue its goals after Roe v. Wade was overturned. Indeed, three more states (Nevada, Virginia, and Missouri) saw abortion-related statewide ballot measures go against pro-lifers in 2026. The recriminations have been bitter against the leaders and key advocacy groups on the pro-life side: They are political naifs; they are incompetent at messaging and strategy; they are self-notable, wannabe big shots who just want proximity to power; they are too focused on federal politics; their organizations’ CEOs make too much money (hilariously false — ask me how I know) for too little results.

    There is plenty of blame to go around, but I think such critiques are missing the key, practical problems the pro-life movement faces. The reality is that the pro-abortion side simply has far more money and organization than the pro-life side, and these gaps have been decisive in election after election. Without the funding for political organization and campaigns, pro-lifers simply cannot win.

    John Gerardi is the executive director of Right to Life of Central California in Fresno. A lawyer and the founding CEO and current development director of the Obria Medical Clinics of Central California, he hosts the radio shows and podcasts The John Gerardi Show and Right to Life Radio.

The program has four elite tiers — Silver, Gold, Platinum, and Titanium — and somehow I’m actually going to end the year as a top tier member, it looks like, without having once stepped foot on an Alaska or Hawaiian flight.

    Sources indicate that as I’ve worked my way through the elite ranks, I’ve become eligible for the milestone perks program, whereby you can select perks when passing various elite thresholds. Along those lines, At the higher tiers, one of the choices becomes upgrade certificates, so I’d like to talk about those a bit, as I’m trying to decide whether or not I should select these.

    Recent findings suggest that I’m intrigued by Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates, given the increasingly global route network of Alaska and Hawaiian. At the same time, the execution of this upgrade program definitely leaves a lot to be desired, including the lack of confirmable upgrade availability.

    I have to make a selection soon, so I’d like to talk through the Alaska and Hawaiian upgrade certificate program, and then get some feedback from Atmos Rewards loyalists. The last time I was focused on upgrade certificates at the airline was when Alaska Mileage Proposal had Gold Guest Upgrades as the upgrade currency, and MVP Gold was the top tier status… those were the days!

    Sources indicate that atmos Rewards issues upgrade certificates as part of the Atmos Rewards milestone perks program. This can be unlocked based on how many status points you earn over the course of a calendar year. Let me emphasize that these upgrade certificates are intended for confirming upgrades in advance, and they’re separate from the complimentary space available upgrades offered.

    Specifically, Atmos Rewards members could earn upgrade certificates at the following thresholds:.

    Titanium status requires 135,000 status points, and I expect to end the year with roughly that many status points. That means I could select up to eight upgrade certificates. However, that would come at the opportunity cost of 70,000 bonus points, for example. Of course I could also mix and match, like selecting four upgrade certificates and 50,000 bonus points.

    Industry observers note that now let’s talk a bit about the rules for redeeming Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates, at least on paper. Upgrades are valid across the Alaska and Hawaiian route networks, and fall into one of two categories:.

    Upgrade certificates can be shared with others, but of course can’t be bartered or sold. One other interesting quirk is that if you cancel or change an itinerary that was upgraded, the certificate will be forfeited. However, a replacement upgrade certificate code can be requested through customer care. Let’s cover the details of upgrades based on the region.

    When it comes to upgrading within North America, an Atmos Rewards upgrade certificate can be confirmed at the time of booking, as long as the “U” fare class is available. If it’s not available, the upgrade will be waitlisted.

    It has been revealed that to cover the very basics, the upgrade certificate is valid for one-way travel (with no connections longer than four hours), for tickets issued by and flown on Alaska and Hawaiian. Tickets purchased in Y, B, H, K, M, L, V, S, or N fare classes, are eligible for upgrades using certificates, while tickets purchased in Q, O, G, or X fare classes, are not eligible.

    To search if a flight is upgrade eligible, select “Upgrade Certificate” in the dropdown in the “Upgrade type” section, during the booking process.

    Then on the search results page, you should be looking for two things:.

    When it comes to upgrading outside of North America, Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates have completely different rules, both for better and worse. First, it’s worth understanding that an upgrade requires either one or two upgrade certificates, depending on the route, per the below chart.

    When it comes to using Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates on global (non-North America) flights, there are both pros and cons:.

    I have to say, the execution of this perk is odd. Keep in mind that Atmos Rewards has a one-of-a-kind upgrade perk for top tier Titanium members, whereby they receive space available upgrades globally on the day of departure. So what’s odd is that if you’re a Titanium member you’re eligible for a complimentary upgrade close to departure, but having applied an upgrade certificate previously gives you no priority. You’d think they’d prioritize members who requested an upgrade, but I suspect it’s a technology limitation of some sort.

    I’d like to address the question of whether Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates are worth it both broadly, and more specifically to my situation.

    Industry observers note that I hear all the time from Atmos Rewards members who are frustrated by the lack of confirmable upgrade space. And indeed, compared to back in the day, upgrade space that can be confirmed is incredibly limited. At the same time, that’s true across airlines nowadays, given how much better airlines have become at actually selling their first class seats, rather than filling them with those upgrading.

    According to recent reports, for example, looking at the route between my home airport of Miami (MIA) and Seattle (SEA) as far out as the schedule opens, I don’t see a single date that has confirmable upgrade space. Now, you’ll sometimes find confirmable upgrade space up and down the West Coast, especially during off peak times, so I don’t want to suggest it’s impossible to find a confirmable upgrade.

    But just broadly speaking, confirmable upgrades with “U” class available for transcontinental and Hawaii flights are exceedingly rare, and it’s like winning the lottery. So it’s really hard to get excited about that.

    In theory, I of course love the idea of being able to upgrade a long haul flight with upgrade certificates. The catch is that an upgrade clearing at most 72 hours before departure really limits flexibility. I suppose you could always apply an upgrade, hope it clears, and then cancel your ticket if it doesn’t, but this would be a last minute scramble.

    Industry observers note that to me, that’s just too risky. It’s not that I’d be unwilling to fly economy on a long haul flight, but by strategically using points, it’s really not necessary in a vast majority of situations, at least based on my own travel patterns.

    The thing is, it’s also notable to view Atmos Rewards upgrade certificates in terms of the opportunity cost of selecting them.

    For example, as I mentioned above, at 55,000 status points I can select two upgrade certificates or 5,000 bonus points. At an opportunity cost of 2,500 points per upgrade certificate, I think it might be worth selecting upgrade certificates. Based on my latest points valuations, I consider Atmos Rewards points to be worth 1.5 cents each, so the opportunity cost per upgrade is $37.50. That’s a rate at which I’d probably be happy to gamble, because if the upgrades expire, it’s not the end of the world.

    According to recent reports, meanwhile at 95,000 status points, the opportunity cost becomes 7,500 bonus points per upgrade, so that’s a value of $112.50 per upgrade. Then at 125,000 status points, the opportunity cost becomes 12,500 bonus points per upgrade, so that’s a value of $187.50. That’s the point at which I’m definitely more inclined to take the “sure thing,” rather than take my chances with an upgrade.

    Atmos Rewards lets members select upgrade certificates as part of the milestone perks program. This always comes at an opportunity cost, and is a better value at some tiers than others.

    Upgrade certificates can be used on Alaska and Hawaiian flights globally, with most one-ways requiring one upgrade certificate, though some global routes requiring two upgrade certificates. While upgrades within North America can be confirmed at the time of booking (pending upgrade availability), global upgrades can only be confirmed at most 72 hours before departure.

    The massive matter with upgrades is the lack of availability. Alaska is just really bad about making confirmed upgrades available, and upgrades clearing at most 72 hours before departure on global flights is less than ideal.

    CodePink co-founder's $55M foundation reinstated in California amid grant questions
